The Explanation of Surah Maryam

This surah is Meccan by consensus, except for the prostration verse within it. One group said it is Meccan, and another group said it is Medinan.

His statement, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾ ﴿The mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariyya﴾ ﴿when he called upon his Lord with a private call﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened, and my head has flared with white hair. And I have never been unsuccessful in my supplication to You, my Lord."﴾ ﴿And indeed I fear the successors after me, and my wife is barren, so grant me from Yourself an heir﴾ ﴿who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub, and make him, my Lord, pleasing.﴾

People differed about the letters that occur at the beginnings of surahs, on two views. One group said they are the secret of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, in the Qur'an. One should not occupy oneself with them. One believes in their outward form and leaves their inner meaning. The majority said: rather, one should speak about them and seek their meanings, for the Arabs sometimes use a single letter to indicate a word, and there is nothing in the Book of Allah that cannot be understood. Then this majority differed over several opinions, which we have already fully discussed in Surah al-Baqarah. Now we mention what is specific to this surah.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: these are letters indicating names of the names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The Kaf is from "Kabir" (Great). Ibn Jubayr also said: the Kaf is from "Kafi" (Sufficient). He also said: it is from "Karim" (Generous).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The implication of their statements is that these letters indicate every name of His, Exalted, that contains a Kaf among His names. They said: the Ha is from "Hadi" (Guide), the Ya is from "'Aliyy" (Most High), and it was said: from "Hakim" (Wise). Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: it is from "Ya'mann la yujir wa la yujar 'alayhi" (He who grants security, does not give protection, and is not given protection against Him). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: the 'Ayn is from "'Aziz" (Mighty). It was said: from "'Alim" (Knowing). It was said: from "'Adl" (Just). The Sad is from "Sadiq" (Truthful). Qatadah said: rather, "Kahay'as" in its entirety is a name for the surah. Another group said: rather, it is one of the names of Allah, Blessed and Exalted. It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to say: "O Kahay'as, forgive me."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This may mean that the whole phrase is among the names of Allah, Exalted. It may also mean that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, intended to call upon Allah, Exalted, with all the names contained in "Kahay'as", as if he meant to say: "O Karim, O Hadi, O 'Ali, O 'Aziz, O Sadiq, forgive me," and he gathered all this in brevity in his saying: "O Kahay'as." Ibn al-Mustanir and others said: "Kahay'as" is an expression for the letters of the alphabet, and al-Zajjaj attributed this to most of the people of the Arabic language. That is, these letters are from them the mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariyya.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this basis the statement of the one who says that "Dhikr" is raised as a predicate of "Kahay'as" is constructed, and these are letters of spelling that are pronounced with a sukun when stopped upon.

All read "Kaf" with the alif and the fa' retained. Nafi' read "the Ha and the Ya" with an intermediate vowel between kasra and fatha, and did not assimilate the dal into the dhal. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' also read with fatha on the Ha and the Ya. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read with damma on the Ha and fatha on the Ya, and it is narrated from him that he read the Ya with damma. It is also narrated from him that he read "Kaf" with damma on the fa'. Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: the meaning of the damma on the Ha and the Ya is the prolongation of emphatic pronunciation, not a pure damma which would necessitate conversion. Abu 'Amr read with kasra on the Ha and fatha on the Ya. 'Asim read with kasra on it. A group read with the clear pronunciation of the nun in "'Ayn" (i.e., 'Ayn-n), and this is the reading of Hafs from 'Asim, and it is the analogical reading, since these are separated letters. All read "'Ayn" with the nun concealed, treating them as if they were connected. Most read with clear pronunciation of the dal in "Sad". Abu 'Amr read with its assimilation into the dhal of his saying "Dhikr". Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read with clear pronunciation of all these letters and separation of each from the others.

His statement "Dhikr" is raised, according to one group, by His statement "Kahay'as", and the reason for that has already been mentioned. Another group said it is raised as the predicate of an implied subject, its estimate being: "This is the mention". Another group said it is raised by the inchoative with an implied predicate, its estimate being: "What has been revealed to you is the mention". Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Ibn Ya'mur read: "Dhakkara rahmata rabbika", with fatha on the dhal, the kaf (shaddah-ed) and the ra', meaning: this recited (text) reminded of the mercy of your Lord to His servant. Whoever says "there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech" has gone to an unnatural extreme. The majority read: "Zakariyya" with the long vowel, and al-A'mash, Yahya and Talhah read "Zakariyya" with the short vowel. Both are dialects, and there are other dialects besides them.

His statement, Exalted: "nada" (called) means: with supplication and desire. People differed about the meaning of his concealing this call. Ibn Jurayj said: that is because hidden deeds are better and further from ostentation (riya'). From this is the Prophet's statement, ﷺ: "The best remembrance is the hidden." Others said: concealment is recommended between the servant and his Master in supplication that is in the sense of pardon and forgiveness, because it indicates from the person that he is good, so concealing it is further from ostentation. As for the supplication and request of Zakariyya, it was about a worldly matter, namely the request for a child, so his concealment was only so that people would not blame him for that, and so that, from the start, if he was answered he would attain his desire, and if he was not answered no one would know of it. It is said: he was described with concealment because it was in the middle of the night.

"Wahana" means: weakened; and weakness in a person or a matter is frailty. Al-A'mash read "wahina" with kasra on the ha'. "Ishta'ala" is used metaphorically for white hair, from the kindling of fire, by way of comparison with it. "Shayban" is in the accusative as an absolute object (masdar) according to the one who regards "ishta'ala" as meaning "shabba" (grew white), and as a specification (tamyiz) according to the one who does not regard it so, but takes it as a different verb. So the matter, for him, is like the Arabs' saying: "wamtala'at ghaythan" (she was filled with anger).

His statement: ﴿and I have never been unsuccessful in my supplication to You, my Lord﴾ is a thanks to Allah, Exalted, for His past favors toward him. Its meaning: You have done good to me in what has passed, and I was made happy by my supplication to You. Bounty requires that its last part should follow its first.

His statement, Exalted: ﴿And indeed I fear the successors﴾ (the verse). People differed about the reason for which he feared the successors. Ibn 'Amir, Mujahid, Qatadah and Abu Salih said: he feared that they would inherit his wealth, and that the kalala (collateral heirs) would inherit it, so he was apprehensive about that. Qatadah and al-Hasan narrated from the Prophet, ﷺ, that he said: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Zakariyya; what was upon him from one who would inherit his wealth." Another group said: rather, his successors were neglectful of the religion, so he feared that upon his death the religion would be lost, and he sought a guardian who would uphold the religion after him. Al-Zajjaj related this view. Its flaw is that it is not permissible for Zakariyya to ask who would inherit his wealth, since prophets are not inherited from.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This supports the Prophet's statement, ﷺ: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from; what we leave is charity." It weakens it that he mentioned the barren wife, and most of the exegetes hold that he meant the inheritance of wealth. The Prophet's statement, ﷺ: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from" may be understood not in a general sense, but as the prevailing state of their affairs, so consider this carefully. The more apparent and more fitting for Zakariyya, peace be upon him, is that he meant the inheritance of knowledge and religion, so that "inheritance" is metaphorical. Do you not see that he only asked for a guardian and did not specify a son, and Allah granted him his hope in the most complete manner? Abu Salih and others said: his statement "who will inherit me" means wealth, and his statement "and inherit from the family of Ya'qub" means knowledge and prophethood. Al-Suddi said: Zakariyya desired a child.

"Khiftu" (I feared) is from fear, and it is the reading of the majority, and this tafsir is based on it. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-'As, Ibn Ya'mur, Ibn Jubayr, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn and others read: "Khaffati" with fatha on the kha', fatha on the fa' with shaddah, kasra on the ta', and with the verb ascribed to "al-mawali" (the successors). The meaning according to this: my supporters (awliya') have ceased and died. On this reading he only asked for a guardian who would uphold the religion. "Al-mawali" are the paternal cousins and relatives who are closest by lineage. His statement ﴿from behind me﴾ means: after me in time. They are "the behind" (al-wara') according to what we explained in Surah al-Kahf. Abu 'Ubaydah said regarding this verse: that is, from between my hands and from in front of me, and this is poor precision. Ibn Kathir read: "min warā'iy" with a long vowel, hamza, and fatha on the ya'. Ibn Kathir also read: "min waraya" with a fatha-ed ya' like "'asaya" (my staff). The rest read with hamza, long vowel, and sukun on the ya'.

"Al-'aqir" (barren) is a woman who does not bear children without being old; likewise a barren man. From this is the statement of 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl:

"Wretched is the youth if I am one-eyed, barren, and cowardly; what excuse have I before every gathering?"

As for Zakariyya, peace be upon him, seeing his condition, he only sought a guardian, and he did not state "a child" plainly, because that was remote in his view on account of the woman. Then he described the guardian with the attribute that was his aim, namely that he should be an heir. A group said: rather, he sought a child, then stipulated that the answer should be that he would live until he inherited from him, guarding against the possibility that the answer would come in the form of a child who dies young and thus the intended purpose would not be attained.

The majority read: "yarithuni wa yarithu" with the verbs in the nominative as a description of the guardian. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read: "yarithni wa yarith" with the verbs in the jussive. According to the school of Sibawayh this is not the answer to "hab" (grant); rather, its estimate is: if you grant him, he will inherit me. The first is more correct in meaning, because he asked for a described heir, and the jussive is weakened by the fact that not every one granted inherits. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others read: "yarithuni warithun min Ali Ya'qub" (an heir from the family of Ya'qub will inherit me). Abu al-Fath said: this is the meaning of the isolation (tajrid), the estimate being: an heir from him or by him will inherit me. Mujahid read: "yarithuni wa yarith" in diminutive form. His statement, Exalted: ﴿from the family of Ya'qub﴾ means from them: wisdom, knowledge and prophethood, and inheritance in all of this is metaphorical. "Radiyy" means: "mardiyy" (pleasing), so it is a fa'il in the sense of maf'ul (passive).

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Its meaning: You have done good to me in what has passed, and I was made happy by my supplication to You. Bounty requires that its last part should follow its first.

Ibn 'Amir, Mujahid, Qatadah and Abu Salih said: he feared that they would inherit his wealth, and that the kalala (collateral heirs) would inherit it, so he was apprehensive about that. Qatadah and al-Hasan narrated from the Prophet, ﷺ, that he said: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Zakariyya; what was upon him from one who would inherit his wealth." Al-Zajjaj related this view. Its flaw is that it is not permissible for Zakariyya to ask who would inherit his wealth, since prophets are not inherited from.

This supports the Prophet's statement, ﷺ: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from; what we leave is charity." They are "the behind" (al-wara') according to what we explained in Surah al-Kahf. Abu 'Ubaydah said regarding this verse: that is, from between my hands and from in front of me, and this is poor precision. Ibn Kathir read: "min warā'iy" with a long vowel, hamza, and fatha on the ya'. Ibn Kathir also read: "min waraya" with a fatha-ed ya' like "'asaya" (my staff). The rest read with hamza, long vowel, and sukun on the ya'.

"Wretched is the youth if I am one-eyed, barren, and cowardly; what excuse have I before every gathering?"

As for Zakariyya, peace be upon him, seeing his condition, he only sought a guardian, and he did not state "a child" plainly, because that was remote in his view on account of the woman. Then he described the guardian with the attribute that was his aim, namely that he should be an heir. A group said: rather, he sought a child, then stipulated that the answer should be that he would live until he inherited from him, guarding against the possibility that the answer would come in the form of a child who dies young and thus the intended purpose would not be attained.

The majority read: "yarithuni wa yarithu" with the verbs in the nominative as a description of the guardian. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read: "yarithni wa yarith" with the verbs in the jussive. According to the school of Sibawayh this is not the answer to "hab" (grant); rather, its estimate is: if you grant him, he will inherit me. The first is more correct in meaning, because he asked for a described heir, and the jussive is weakened by the fact that not every one granted inherits. His statement, Exalted: ﴿from the family of Ya'qub﴾ means from them: wisdom, knowledge and prophethood, and inheritance in all of this is metaphorical. "Radiyy" means: "mardiyy" (pleasing), so it is a fa'il in the sense of maf'ul (passive).

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The Explanation of Surah Maryam

This surah is Meccan by consensus, except for the prostration verse within it. One group said it is Meccan, and another group said it is Medinan.

His statement, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾ ﴿The mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariyya﴾ ﴿when he called upon his Lord with a private call﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened, and my head has flared with white hair. And I have never been unsuccessful in my supplication to You, my Lord."﴾ ﴿And indeed I fear the successors after me, and my wife is barren, so grant me from Yourself an heir﴾ ﴿who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub, and make him, my Lord, pleasing.﴾

People differed about the letters that occur at the beginnings of surahs, on two views. One group said they are the secret of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, in the Qur'an. One should not occupy oneself with them. One believes in their outward form and leaves their inner meaning. The majority said: rather, one should speak about them and seek their meanings, for the Arabs sometimes use a single letter to indicate a word, and there is nothing in the Book of Allah that cannot be understood. Then this majority differed over several opinions, which we have already fully discussed in Surah al-Baqarah. Now we mention what is specific to this surah.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: these are letters indicating names of the names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The Kaf is from "Kabir" (Great). Ibn Jubayr also said: the Kaf is from "Kafi" (Sufficient). He also said: it is from "Karim" (Generous).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The implication of their statements is that these letters indicate every name of His, Exalted, that contains a Kaf among His names. They said: the Ha is from "Hadi" (Guide), the Ya is from "'Aliyy" (Most High), and it was said: from "Hakim" (Wise). Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: it is from "Ya'mann la yujir wa la yujar 'alayhi" (He who grants security, does not give protection, and is not given protection against Him). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: the 'Ayn is from "'Aziz" (Mighty). It was said: from "'Alim" (Knowing). It was said: from "'Adl" (Just). The Sad is from "Sadiq" (Truthful). Qatadah said: rather, "Kahay'as" in its entirety is a name for the surah. Another group said: rather, it is one of the names of Allah, Blessed and Exalted. It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to say: "O Kahay'as, forgive me."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This may mean that the whole phrase is among the names of Allah, Exalted. It may also mean that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, intended to call upon Allah, Exalted, with all the names contained in "Kahay'as", as if he meant to say: "O Karim, O Hadi, O 'Ali, O 'Aziz, O Sadiq, forgive me," and he gathered all this in brevity in his saying: "O Kahay'as." Ibn al-Mustanir and others said: "Kahay'as" is an expression for the letters of the alphabet, and al-Zajjaj attributed this to most of the people of the Arabic language. That is, these letters are from them the mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariyya.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this basis the statement of the one who says that "Dhikr" is raised as a predicate of "Kahay'as" is constructed, and these are letters of spelling that are pronounced with a sukun when stopped upon.

All read "Kaf" with the alif and the fa' retained. Nafi' read "the Ha and the Ya" with an intermediate vowel between kasra and fatha, and did not assimilate the dal into the dhal. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' also read with fatha on the Ha and the Ya. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read with damma on the Ha and fatha on the Ya, and it is narrated from him that he read the Ya with damma. It is also narrated from him that he read "Kaf" with damma on the fa'. Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: the meaning of the damma on the Ha and the Ya is the prolongation of emphatic pronunciation, not a pure damma which would necessitate conversion. Abu 'Amr read with kasra on the Ha and fatha on the Ya. 'Asim read with kasra on it. A group read with the clear pronunciation of the nun in "'Ayn" (i.e., 'Ayn-n), and this is the reading of Hafs from 'Asim, and it is the analogical reading, since these are separated letters. All read "'Ayn" with the nun concealed, treating them as if they were connected. Most read with clear pronunciation of the dal in "Sad". Abu 'Amr read with its assimilation into the dhal of his saying "Dhikr". Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read with clear pronunciation of all these letters and separation of each from the others.

His statement "Dhikr" is raised, according to one group, by His statement "Kahay'as", and the reason for that has already been mentioned. Another group said it is raised as the predicate of an implied subject, its estimate being: "This is the mention". Another group said it is raised by the inchoative with an implied predicate, its estimate being: "What has been revealed to you is the mention". Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Ibn Ya'mur read: "Dhakkara rahmata rabbika", with fatha on the dhal, the kaf (shaddah-ed) and the ra', meaning: this recited (text) reminded of the mercy of your Lord to His servant. Whoever says "there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech" has gone to an unnatural extreme. The majority read: "Zakariyya" with the long vowel, and al-A'mash, Yahya and Talhah read "Zakariyya" with the short vowel. Both are dialects, and there are other dialects besides them.

The commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 19, verses 7–11:

Allah the Exalted said:

﴿O Zakariyya, indeed We give you good tidings of a boy whose name is Yahya; We have not assigned to anyone before him the same name.﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, how can I have a boy when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age?"﴾ ﴿He said: "So it will be. Your Lord says: 'It is easy for Me, and I created you before, when you were nothing.'"﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, appoint for me a sign." He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three nights, though you are sound."﴾ ﴿So he came out to his people from the mihrab (the niche of prayer, a raised place of worship), and he signaled to them to glorify God morning and evening.﴾

The meaning: He was told, right after his supplication: "Indeed We give you good tidings of a boy who will be born to you, whose name is Yahya." The majority (al-Jumhur) read "nubashshiruka" with a fatha on the ba' and a kasra on the shin, doubled. The companions of Ibn Mas'ud read "nabshuruka" with a sukun on the ba' and a damma on the shin.

Qatada said: He was named Yahya because Allah gave him life (ahyahu) through prophethood and faith. Some said: He was named so because Allah gave life through him to people by means of religious commitment. The word "samiyyan" in the language means: We have not made for him a partner in this name, that is, no one was previously named Yahya. This is the view of Qatada, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Aslam and al-Suddi. Mujahid and others said: "samiyyan" means a like or an equal.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This seems to derive from the sense of "competing in eminence" (al-musamah wa al-sumuww), but this is far-fetched, because he does not surpass Ibrahim and Musa, peace be upon them both, except that he surpasses them in a specific respect, in nobility and restraint.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, said: The meaning is that barren women have not borne one like him.

As for Zakariyya's statement: "How can I have a boy?", people differed about it. One group said: He was only asking for an heir (waliyy), without specifying a son. When he was given good tidings of a son, he asked how this would come about given these obstacles. Another group said: He was asking for a son while he was in a state in which he hoped for a son through marriage to a non-barren woman, or he was given good tidings but his prayer was not answered until a long time had passed, during which he came to the state of one who cannot have children. At that point he asked, and informed about himself, of his old age and decrepitude. Another group said: Rather, he asked for a son, and when he was given good tidings of it at the time of the supplication, he sought understanding by way of question, not by way of doubt: How is the path to this achieved? How does the decree come to pass through him? This was not that it seemed far-fetched to him in the power of Allah.

Al-'Itiyy and al-'Usiyy mean extreme old age, and the dryness of a stick, or the whiteness of the head, or something similar. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "'itiyyan" with a kasra on the ayn, and the rest read it with a damma. Ibn Mas'ud read "'taiyyan" with a fatha on the ayn. Abu Hatim related that Ibn Mas'ud read "'usiyyan" with a damma on the ayn and with a sin. Al-Dani also related it from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, that he said: I do not know whether the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to recite in the Zuhr and 'Asr prayers, and I do not know whether he recited "'itiyyan" or "'usiyyan" with a sin. Al-Tabari also related from al-Suddi that he said: Jibril called out to Zakariyya: "Indeed Allah gives you good tidings of a boy whose name is Yahya." Then Satan met him and said to him: That voice was not from an angel; it was from a devil. At that Zakariyya said: "How can I have a boy?", to confirm that it came from Allah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Zakariyya was of the descendants of Harun, peace be upon him. Qatada said: This matter happened to him when he was about seventy-some years old; it was said he was seventy; al-Zajjaj said he was sixty-five.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It had overcome his assumption that he would not have a child.

As for His saying: ﴿He said: "So it will be,"﴾ it was said: The meaning is that the angel said to him: "So let existence be," just as it was said to you: "Your Lord says: the creation of the boy is easy for Me," that is, it is not unprecedented; and just as I created you before and brought you from non-existence into existence, so I do now... Al-Tabari said: The meaning of His saying "kadhalika" is: the two matters you mentioned, the barren woman and extreme age, are so, but your Lord has said [it is easy].

(p-12) The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

My own understanding of the meaning is: the angel said "kadhalika," that is, in this state your Lord said: it is easy for Me.

The majority read "wa-qad khalaqtuka," and Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "wa-qad khalaqnaka." As for His exalted saying: ﴿and you were not anything﴾, that means: you were not existing. Zakariyya said: "My Lord, appoint for me a sign," that is, a token by which I may know the truth of this and that it is from You. It is related that when Zakariyya, peace be upon him, came to know [the good tidings], then asked for a sign after that, Allah the Exalted punished him by afflicting him with silence from speaking to people. Even if this was not due to an illness (dumbness or the like), there was in it, in every case, some form of punishment. It is related from Ibn Zayd that when Zakariyya's wife conceived Yahya, he became unable to speak to anyone, yet he would recite the Torah and mention Allah; when he wished to converse with anyone, he could not.

It is possible, on this view, that His saying "appoint for me a sign" means: a sign by which I know that the pregnancy has occurred. Al-Zajjaj explained it in this way.

The meaning of His saying "sawiyyan," according to the majority, is: healthy, without any impediment or dumbness. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, also said: this refers to the nights; he meant: complete, even.

As for His exalted saying: ﴿So he came out to his people﴾ [al-Qasas: 79], the meaning is that Allah the Exalted manifested the sign by Zakariyya's coming out of his mihrab, which is the place of prayer. The mihrab is the highest of places and buildings, since it is fortified against whoever opposes it. Then this name was specially given to the building of prayer. They used to make it in the elevated part of the ground. People differed about its derivation: one group said it is derived from war (harb), as if its occupant wages war against Satan and desires; another group said it is derived from "haraba" (with a fatha on the ra'), as if its occupant encounters from it hardship, fatigue and toil. There is something to examine in the wording after this.

As for His saying "fa-awha" (and he signaled), Qatada and Ibn Munabbih said: it was by a gesture. Mujahid said: rather, by writing it in the dust.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Both opinions are revelation (wahy). As for His saying: ﴿that glorify﴾, "an" is explanatory, with the meaning of "i" (that is), (p-13) and "sabbihu" (glorify): Qatada said its meaning is: pray (salli), and "al-subha" is prayer. Another group said: rather, He commanded them to remember Allah and say "Subhan Allah." Talha read "an sabbihuhu" with a pronoun. The rest of the verse is clear.

There is something to examine in the wording after this.

As for His saying "fa-awha" (and he signaled), Qatada and Ibn Munabbih said: it was by a gesture. Mujahid said: rather, by writing it in the dust.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Both opinions are revelation (wahy). As for His saying: ﴿that glorify﴾, "an" is explanatory, with the meaning of "i" (that is), (p-13) and "sabbihu" (glorify): Qatada said its meaning is: pray (salli), and "al-subha" is prayer. Another group said: rather, He commanded them to remember Allah and say "Subhan Allah." Talha read "an sabbihuhu" with a pronoun. The rest of the verse is clear.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

In the word "boy" according to this view there is a figurative usage and a retention of a previous state.

Mujahid said: Yahya's food was grass, and there were permanent channels for tears on his cheek. Among the evidences for "hanan" is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

؎ And the sons of Shamaja ibn Jirm grant them their goats, "hananaka, O possessor of hanan"

And the saying of al-Nabigha:

؎ O Abu Mundhir, you have exhausted us, so spare some of us *** "hananayka, some evil is easier than some evil"

And another said:

؎ She said: "Hanan, what brought you here?" *** "Are you of a lineage, or are you acquainted with the tribe?"

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and dutiful to his parents, and he was not arrogant or disobedient﴾: "al-barr" is one who has much piety; "al-jabbar" is the arrogant one, as if he compels people to his character; "al-jabbarah" is the tall, great palm tree. The nobility lies in God greeting him and honoring him in the situations in which a person is in extreme weakness, need, lack of resource, poverty before God, and great terror.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 19, verses 16–20:**

God the Exalted says:

﴿And mention in the Book Mary, when she withdrew from her family to a place in the east.﴾ ﴿And she took a screen apart from them, and We sent to her Our Spirit, and it presented itself to her as a man in every respect.﴾ ﴿She said, "I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing."﴾ ﴿He said, "I am only a messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy."﴾ ﴿She said, "How can I have a boy when no man has touched me and I have not been unchaste?"﴾

This is the beginning of a new story, not part of the previous one. The address is to Muhammad (ﷺ). "The Book" is the Qur'an. "Maryam" is the daughter of 'Imran, the mother of 'Isa (Jesus), and the sister of the mother of Yahya (John). People differed about why she withdrew. The word *intibadh* (withdrawal) means to remove oneself. Al-Suddi said: she withdrew in order to purify herself from menstruation. Others said: in order to worship God.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is the better view. Mary had been dedicated to the service (*sadana*, guardianship) of the place of worship, its service and devotion, so she withdrew from people for this purpose. His words, ﴿a place in the east﴾, mean in the direction of the east from the dwellings of her family. The reason for it being in the east is that they used to honour the direction of the east, from where the lights rise, and the eastern directions of everything were considered superior to others. This was related by al-Tabari, may God have mercy on him.

'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: "I know better than people why the Christians took the east as their *qibla*, because of the words of God the Exalted: ﴿when she withdrew from her family to a place in the east﴾, so they took the birthplace of 'Isa as their *qibla*." Some people said: the screen (*hijab*) she took was for concealing herself from people in order to worship. Al-Suddi said it was of walls; it was also said it was of garments. Some exegetes said: she took the place to the east of the *mihrab* (prayer niche).

The "Spirit" (*ruh*) is Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him; it was also said to be 'Isa. Al-Zajjaj related both views. Whoever says it is Jibril takes the sentence to mean: then he (Jibril) presented himself to her. Whoever says it is 'Isa takes the sentence to mean: then the angel presented himself to her. Al-Naqqash said: whoever reads *"Ruhanna"* with a doubled *nun* makes it the name of one of the angels.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

I have not seen this reading attributed to anyone else.

People differed about whether Maryam was a prophetess. It was said: she was a prophetess, by this sending and by her conversation with the angel. It was also said: she was not a prophetess; rather, a figure in the form of a man spoke to her, and her seeing an angel was like the way Jibril was seen in the form of Dihya, and in his asking about Islam. The first view is more apparent.

As for God's words, ﴿She said, "I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing."﴾ the meaning is: Maryam said to the angel who had presented himself to her as a man, when she saw that he had broken through the screen she had taken, and so she thought ill of him: "I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are a person of piety." Abu Wa'il said: she knew that the God-fearing person has restraint. Wahb ibn Munabbih, may God be pleased with him, said: she meant the name of a wicked man who was among her people in that time. When she saw him climbing over the wall towards her, she thought he was that man, so she sought refuge in the Most Merciful from him. Makki, may God have mercy on him, and others related this. It is weak and goes along with conjecture.

The angel said to her: "So it is, as I have described. But [the verb] 'said' is [in the form] 'your Lord said,' and it is possible that he means: 'In this condition your Lord said.' The meaning is close either way." The word *al-āyah* ("sign") means a lesson presented for consideration. The pronoun in His words *linajʿalahu* ("that We may make him") refers to the boy. *Wa-raḥmatan minnā* ("and a mercy from Us") means: a path of guidance for a great many people, through which they attain mercy. Then he informed her that the matter had been decreed and carried out. The word *al-amr* ("matter") here is the singular of *al-umūr* (affairs), and it is not the verbal noun of *amara yaʾmuru* (to command).

It is reported that Jibril, peace be upon him, when he exchanged this conversation with her, blew into the opening of her garment, and the breath traveled, by Allah's permission, until she conceived from it. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih and others. Ibn Jurayj said: he blew into the opening of her garment and her palm. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the breath that was blown entered through her mouth. This is His words: ﴿so she conceived him﴾, meaning she conceived the boy.

It is also mentioned that she was thirteen years old. When she sensed this and feared the people's reproach and that evil would be attributed to her, she withdrew with him, meaning she moved away to a distant place out of modesty and fleeing with her face [turned away]. It is reported in this regard that she fled to the land of Egypt or somewhere near it, as said by Wahb ibn Munabbih. It is also reported that she went out to a place known as Bayt Lahm, which lay four miles from Iliya.

The word *ajāʾahā* means: it compelled her. *Ajāʾa* is the causative of *jāʾa* by means of the hamzah. Shibl ibn ʿAzrah read *fājaʾahā* (it surprised her), from *al-mufājaʾah* (suddenness), and this is also reported from ʿĀṣim. In the *muṣḥaf* (copy of the Qur'an) of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb it reads: *falammā ajāʾahā al-makhāḍu* (when the pains compelled her). Zuhayr said:

*A traveler who journeyed intent upon you, fear and hope compelled him.*

The majority read *al-makhāḍa* with a fatḥah on the mīm. Ibn Kathir, as is reported from him, read it with a kasrah, and it means the labor pains and the intensity of childbirth and its agonies. It is reported that she reached a place where there was a dry, withered palm trunk at whose base was a cattle trough beside a flowing stream. The matter grew severe for her there, she embraced the trunk because of the intensity of the pain, and she gave birth to ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. At the time of her delivery, because of the pains she saw, the estrangement, the denial of her people, and the difficulty of the situation from every direction, she said: "Would that I had died and this decree had not come upon me."

Al-Ḥasan, Abū Jaʿfar, Shaybah, ʿĀṣim, Abū ʿAmr, and a group read *muttu* with a ḍammah on the mīm. Al-Aʿraj, Ṭalḥah, Yaḥyā, and al-Aʿmash read it with a kasrah, and the reading from Nāfiʿ varies. Maryam wished for death from the standpoint of religion, since she feared that evil would be attributed to her regarding her religion, and that she would be reproached, and that this would tempt her. In this same sense ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, and a group of the righteous wished for death. The Prophet's ﷺ prohibition of wishing for death applies only to harm that befalls the body. He, ﷺ, permitted it in his words:

"A time will come upon people when a man will pass by the grave of another and say: 'Would that I were in his place.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: because it is a time of trials to religion.

She said: ﴿and I was something forgotten and utterly forgotten﴾, meaning a thing abandoned and despised. In the speech of the Arabs, *al-nasy* is a worthless thing whose nature is to be forgotten, so that no one grieves over its loss, like a stake or a rope for the traveler and the like. It is said *nasyun* and *nisyun*, with a fatḥah and a kasrah on the nūn. The majority read it with a kasrah. Ḥamzah alone read it with a fatḥah, and the reading from ʿĀṣim varies. Like Ḥamzah's reading, Ṭalḥah, al-Aʿmash, and Yaḥyā read it. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī read *nisʾan* with a hamzah and a kasrah on the nūn. Nawf al-Bikālī read *nasʾan* with a fatḥah on the nūn; Abū al-Fatḥ and Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī transmitted this from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī. Bakr ibn Ḥabīb read *nassan* with a shaddah on the sīn and a fatḥah on the nūn, without a hamzah. Al-Shanfarā said:

*It is as if for her on the earth is a trace (nass) that she follows, and when she is nourished, and if she speaks to you, she is confused.*

Al-Ṭabarī, in relating her story, mentioned that when she conceived ʿĪsā, her sister also conceived Yaḥyā. Her sister came to visit her and said: "O Maryam, did you know that I have conceived?" Maryam said to her: "Did you know that I have conceived?" She said to her: "I find that what is in my belly prostrates to what is in your belly." This is because it is reported that she sensed her fetus lowering its head toward the side of Maryam's belly. Al-Suddī said: this is His, exalted is He, words: ﴿confirming a word from Allah﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 39].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: all of this is weak, so consider it carefully. Al-Ṭabarī also mentioned from her story that she went out fleeing with a man from the Children of Israel named Yūsuf the Carpenter, who used to serve the mosque with her. Al-Ṭabarī elaborated on this, but I have abridged it because of its weakness. This story implies that she conceived and remained pregnant in the customary manner of women, that she felt shame because of it and fled because of it while pregnant. This is the view of the majority of the commentators. It is reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: there was nothing but that she conceived and gave birth in a single hour. And Allah knows best.

It was also said that she bore him after seven months, and it was said after six months.

God Almighty said:

﴿He said: "So it will be. Your Lord said: 'It is easy for Me, and so that We may make him a sign for people and a mercy from Us. It is a matter decreed.'"﴾ ﴿So she conceived him, and withdrew with him to a remote place.﴾ ﴿Then the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree. She said: "Would that I had died before this and had become something forgotten and utterly forgotten!"﴾

The angel said to her: "So it is, as I have described. But [the verb] 'said' is [in the form] 'your Lord said,' and it is possible that he means: 'In this condition your Lord said.' The meaning is close either way." The word *al-āyah* ("sign") means a lesson presented for consideration. The pronoun in His words *linajʿalahu* ("that We may make him") refers to the boy. *Wa-raḥmatan minnā* ("and a mercy from Us") means: a path of guidance for a great many people, through which they attain mercy. Then he informed her that the matter had been decreed and carried out. The word *al-amr* ("matter") here is the singular of *al-umūr* (affairs), and it is not the verbal noun of *amara yaʾmuru* (to command).

It is reported that Jibril, peace be upon him, when he exchanged this conversation with her, blew into the opening of her garment, and the breath traveled, by Allah's permission, until she conceived from it. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih and others. Ibn Jurayj said: he blew into the opening of her garment and her palm. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the breath that was blown entered through her mouth. This is His words: ﴿so she conceived him﴾, meaning she conceived the boy.

It is also mentioned that she was thirteen years old. When she sensed this and feared the people's reproach and that evil would be attributed to her, she withdrew with him, meaning she moved away to a distant place out of modesty and fleeing with her face [turned away]. It is reported in this regard that she fled to the land of Egypt or somewhere near it, as said by Wahb ibn Munabbih. It is also reported that she went out to a place known as Bayt Lahm, which lay four miles from Iliya.

The word *ajāʾahā* means: it compelled her. *Ajāʾa* is the causative of *jāʾa* by means of the hamzah. Shibl ibn ʿAzrah read *fājaʾahā* (it surprised her), from *al-mufājaʾah* (suddenness), and this is also reported from ʿĀṣim. In the *muṣḥaf* (copy of the Qur'an) of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb it reads: *falammā ajāʾahā al-makhāḍu* (when the pains compelled her). Zuhayr said:

*A traveler who journeyed intent upon you, fear and hope compelled him.*

The majority read *al-makhāḍa* with a fatḥah on the mīm. Ibn Kathir, as is reported from him, read it with a kasrah, and it means the labor pains and the intensity of childbirth and its agonies. It is reported that she reached a place where there was a dry, withered palm trunk at whose base was a cattle trough beside a flowing stream. The matter grew severe for her there, she embraced the trunk because of the intensity of the pain, and she gave birth to ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. At the time of her delivery, because of the pains she saw, the estrangement, the denial of her people, and the difficulty of the situation from every direction, she said: "Would that I had died and this decree had not come upon me."

The Prophet's ﷺ prohibition of wishing for death applies only to harm that befalls the body. He, ﷺ, permitted it in his words:

"A time will come upon people when a man will pass by the grave of another and say: 'Would that I were in his place.'"

Bakr ibn Ḥabīb read *nassan* with a shaddah on the sīn and a fatḥah on the nūn, without a hamzah. Al-Shanfarā said:

*It is as if for her on the earth is a trace (nass) that she follows, and when she is nourished, and if she speaks to you, she is confused.*

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 19, verses 24–26:

The words of the Most High:

﴿Then he called to her from beneath her: "Do not grieve; your Lord has placed beneath you a stream."﴾ ﴿And shake toward yourself the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you fresh ripe dates.﴾ ﴿So eat and drink and be content. And if you see any human, say: "I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak today to any human being."﴾

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Zayd ibn Hubaysh, Mujahid, al-Jahdari and a group read "فَناداها مَن تَحْتَها" (fanadahā man taḥtahā), with "man" as the subject of "yunadi" (called), and the intended "man" is 'Isa (peace be upon him), i.e., the newborn called to her. This was said by Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him both) said the intended one is Jibril (peace be upon him), and that he did not speak until she brought him to her people. 'Alqamah, al-Dahhak and Qatadah said: in this there is a sign for her and an indication that this is one of the extraordinary matters outside the normal course, in which Allah has a great purpose, especially since the one calling is 'Isa, for by him the excuse of Maryam is made clear and no doubt remains about her. Therefore the call was that she should not grieve.

Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, al-Dahhak, 'Amr ibn Maymun, the people of Medina, the people of Kufa, 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him both) also, and al-Hasan read "مِن تَحْتِها" (min taḥtihā) with a kasra on the mim, taking it to denote the starting point. They differed: some said the intended one is 'Isa (peace be upon him); a group said the intended one is Jibril, who had been near her before. They said: she was in a wide space of the earth, lower than the spot where she was.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The first view is more apparent, and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan used to hold it.

'Alqamah and Zirr ibn Hubaysh read: "فَخاطَبَها مِن تَحْتِها" (fakhatabahā min taḥtihā), "then he addressed her from beneath her." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him both) read: "فَناداها مَلَكٌ مِن تَحْتِها" (fanadahā malakun min taḥtihā), "then an angel called to her from beneath her."

His words "﴿Do not grieve﴾" explain the call; "أن" (an) here is explanatory, meaning "i.e." (ay). "As-sarī" among men is the noble of qualities, the chief; "as-sarī" also means a stream of water. Accordingly people differed about this verse. Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: it means "He made beneath you a great man of the men, having rank." The majority said: he pointed for her to the stream which was near the trunk of the palm tree. It is related that al-Hasan explained the verse, saying: "Indeed, Allah made him a noble sarī," and Hamid ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Himyari said: "O Abu Sa'id, we only mean by sarī the stream." He said: "I love your nearness for this and its like, but the rulers have overcome us regarding you."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Among the evidence for "sarī" is the verse of Labid:

"So they both crossed the middle of the stream and split it, its bank ... the neighboring of its cuttings..." (poetic verse as in the source)

Then He commanded her to shake the dry trunk so that she might see another sign in the revival of the dead trunk. A group said: the palm tree was grafted and bore ripe dates; al-Suddi said: the trunk was cut, and He caused a river to flow beneath her at that very moment.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The apparent meaning of the verse is that 'Isa was the one speaking to her, and that the trunk was dry; and on this basis they are signs that comfort her and calm her. The "bi" in His words "بِجِذْعِ" (bi-jidh'i) is extra, for emphasis. Abu 'Ali said: like one says "ألقى بيده" (alqā bi-yadihi), i.e., "he cast his hand."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

There is consideration in this example. Al-Tabari (may Allah have mercy on him) cited:

"In a Yemeni valley whose upper part grows the lote tree, and whose lower part [grows] with the brackish and the shubhan..."

Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amr... [note: the next reading list follows], Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, and the majority of people read "تَسّاقَطْ" (tassāqaṭ) with a fatha on the ta and shadda on the sin, referring to the palm tree. al-Bara' ibn 'Azib (may Allah be pleased with him) and al-A'mash (may Allah have mercy on him) read "يَسّاقَطْ" (yassāqaṭ), referring to the trunk. Hamzah alone read "تَساقَطْ" (tasāqaṭ) with a fatha on the ta and a light sin; this is the reading of Masruq, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Talhah ibn Musarrif and Abu 'Amr with variation. A group read "يَسّاقَطْ" (yassāqaṭ) with the ya, referring to the palm tree or the trunk as previously mentioned. 'Asim, in the transmission of Hafs, read "تُساقِطْ" (tusāqiṭ) with a damma on the ta, a fatha on the sin and lightened. Abu Haywah read "يُسْقِطْ" (yusqiṭ) with a damma on the ya. Abu 'Ali related in al-Hujjah that it was read "يَتَساقَطْ" (yatasāqaṭ) with a ya and a ta. It is related from Masruq: "تُسْقِطْ" (tusqiṭ) with a damma on the ta and a kasra on the qaf, and likewise from Abu Haywah. Abu Haywah also read "يَسْقُطْ" (yasquṭ) with a fatha on the ya and a damma on the qaf. "رُطَبٌ جَنِيٌّ" (ruṭabun janiyyun), "fresh ripe dates."

The nasb of "رُطَبًا" (ruṭaban) varies according to the meanings of the readings mentioned: sometimes the verb is attributed to the trunk, sometimes to the shaking, and sometimes to the palm tree. "جَنِيًّا" (janiyyan) means it has ripened and become fit for picking, from "janaytu al-thamarah" (I picked the fruit). Talhah ibn Sulayman read "جِنِيًّا" (jiniyyan) with a kasra on the jim. 'Amr ibn Maymun said: nothing is better for a woman who has just given birth than dates and fresh dates. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "رُطَبًا" (ruṭaban) means 'ajwah (a type of date).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Some people derived from this verse that provision, even if it is decreed, Allah the Exalted has entrusted the son of Adam to strive for what is in it; for Maryam was commanded to shake the trunk so that she would see a sign, and the sign would be in not shaking it.

Al-Tabari related from Ibn Zayd that 'Isa said to her: "Do not grieve," and she said: "How can I not grieve when you are with me? I am not a married woman, so that I could say: from a husband; nor a slave woman, so that I could say: from my master. What excuse will I have before the people? 'Would that I had died before this and become a thing forgotten.'" [Maryam: 23]. Then 'Isa said to her: "I will suffice you in speech."

His words, Exalted is He: "﴿So eat and drink and be content﴾" and the rest of the verse. The majority read "وَقَرِّي" (waqarri) with a fatha on the qaf. Al-Tabari related the reading "وَقِرِّي" (waqirri) with a kasra on the qaf. "Qurrat al-'ayn" (coolness of the eye) is derived from "al-qarr" (coolness), for it is reported that tears of joy are cool and tears of grief are warm. A group weakened this and said: all tears are warm, and the meaning of "qurrat al-'ayn" is that the weeping which heats the eye has ceased, i.e., there is no grief from the matter by which the eye is cooled. Al-Shaybani said: "وَقَرِّي عَيْنًا" (waqarri 'aynan) means: sleep; he urged her to eat, drink and sleep. The word "عَيْنًا" (aynan) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), and the verb in reality belongs to the eye, so it is transferred to the one who has the eye, and the one who was the actual subject is put in the accusative as an explanation. Similar to "ṭibta nafsan" (you are content in soul), "tafaqqa'ta shaḥman" (you were split open in fat), "taṣabbabtu 'araqan" (I poured out sweat), and this is common.

The majority read "تَرَيِنَّ" (tarayinna), and its origin is "تَرْأيِينَ" (tar'iyīna). The nun was deleted for the jazm, then the vowel of the hamza was transferred to the ra, then the first ya was changed to an alif because it was vowelled and preceded by a fatha; two sakins came together, the alif (converted from ya) and the ya, so the alif was deleted and it became "تَرى" (tara). On this pattern is the verse of al-Afwah:

"If you see my head, its state has harmed it..." (verse continues)

Then the heavy nun entered, and the ya was given a kasra because two sakins came together, from it and from the nun. The nun entered here as a preparation, just as the lam of oath also enters as a preparation. Abu 'Amr, as related from him, read "تَرَئِنَّ" (taraʾinna) with a hamza. Talhah, Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read "تَرَيْنَ" (taraynā) with a sukun on the ya and a light fatha on the nun; Abu al-Fath said: "this is shadhdh (irregular)."

The meaning of this verse is that Allah the Exalted commanded her, through the tongue of Jibril or her son (peace be upon them both), as in the earlier disagreement, that she should refrain from speaking to people, and refer them to her son in that matter, so that her embarrassment would be removed and the sign would be manifest, and her excuse would stand. The apparent meaning of the verse is that she was permitted to say these words that are in the verse; this is the view of the majority. A group said: the meaning of "فَقولي" (faqūlī) is by gesture, not by speech, for otherwise the contradiction in her matter would be evident.

Ibn 'Abbas and Anas ibn Malik read: "إنِّي نَذَرْتُ لِلرَّحْمَنِ وصُمْتُ" (innī nadhartu lil-Raḥmāni wa-ṣumtu), "I have vowed to the Most Merciful and I have fasted." A people said: its meaning is a fast from speech, since the origin of fasting is abstention, and from it is the verse of the poet: "horses that abstain (ṣiyām)..." (verse continues). Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi said: the custom of fasting among them was abstaining from eating and speaking. A group read: "إنِّي نَذَرْتُ لِلرَّحْمَنِ صَمْتًا" (innī nadhartu lil-Raḥmāni ṣamtan), "I have vowed to the Most Merciful silence."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It is not permissible in our law for anyone to vow a fast of this kind; and Ibn Mas'ud commanded whoever did this to speak and talk. A group said: Maryam was commanded with this so that 'Isa would suffice her in argument.

The majority said: he pointed for her to the stream which was near the trunk of the palm tree. He said: "I love your nearness for this and its like, but the rulers have overcome us regarding you."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Among the evidence for "sarī" is the verse of Labid:

"So they both crossed the middle of the stream and split it, its bank ... the neighboring of its cuttings..." (poetic verse as in the source)

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

There is consideration in this example. Al-Tabari (may Allah have mercy on him) cited:

"In a Yemeni valley whose upper part grows the lote tree, and whose lower part [grows] with the brackish and the shubhan..."

Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amr... [note: the next reading list follows], Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, and the majority of people read "تَسّاقَطْ" (tassāqaṭ) with a fatha on the ta and shadda on the sin, referring to the palm tree. al-Bara' ibn 'Azib (may Allah be pleased with him) and al-A'mash (may Allah have mercy on him) read "يَسّاقَطْ" (yassāqaṭ), referring to the trunk. Hamzah alone read "تَساقَطْ" (tasāqaṭ) with a fatha on the ta and a light sin; this is the reading of Masruq, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Talhah ibn Musarrif and Abu 'Amr with variation. A group read "يَسّاقَطْ" (yassāqaṭ) with the ya, referring to the palm tree or the trunk as previously mentioned. 'Asim, in the transmission of Hafs, read "تُساقِطْ" (tusāqiṭ) with a damma on the ta, a fatha on the sin and lightened. Abu Haywah read "يُسْقِطْ" (yusqiṭ) with a damma on the ya. Abu 'Ali related in al-Hujjah that it was read "يَتَساقَطْ" (yatasāqaṭ) with a ya and a ta. It is related from Masruq: "تُسْقِطْ" (tusqiṭ) with a damma on the ta and a kasra on the qaf, and likewise from Abu Haywah. Abu Haywah also read "يَسْقُطْ" (yasquṭ) with a fatha on the ya and a damma on the qaf. "رُطَبٌ جَنِيٌّ" (ruṭabun janiyyun), "fresh ripe dates."

The nasb of "رُطَبًا" (ruṭaban) varies according to the meanings of the readings mentioned: sometimes the verb is attributed to the trunk, sometimes to the shaking, and sometimes to the palm tree. "جَنِيًّا" (janiyyan) means it has ripened and become fit for picking, from "janaytu al-thamarah" (I picked the fruit). Talhah ibn Sulayman read "جِنِيًّا" (jiniyyan) with a kasra on the jim. 'Amr ibn Maymun said: nothing is better for a woman who has just given birth than dates and fresh dates. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "رُطَبًا" (ruṭaban) means 'ajwah (a type of date).

I am not a married woman, so that I could say: from a husband; nor a slave woman, so that I could say: from my master. What excuse will I have before the people? 'Would that I had died before this and become a thing forgotten.'" [Maryam: 23]. Then 'Isa said to her: "I will suffice you in speech."

His words, Exalted is He: "﴿So eat and drink and be content﴾" and the rest of the verse. The majority read "وَقَرِّي" (waqarri) with a fatha on the qaf. Al-Tabari related the reading "وَقِرِّي" (waqirri) with a kasra on the qaf. "Qurrat al-'ayn" (coolness of the eye) is derived from "al-qarr" (coolness), for it is reported that tears of joy are cool and tears of grief are warm. A group weakened this and said: all tears are warm, and the meaning of "qurrat al-'ayn" is that the weeping which heats the eye has ceased, i.e., there is no grief from the matter by which the eye is cooled. Al-Shaybani said: "وَقَرِّي عَيْنًا" (waqarri 'aynan) means: sleep; he urged her to eat, drink and sleep. "If you see my head, its state has harmed it..." (verse continues)

Then the heavy nun entered, and the ya was given a kasra because two sakins came together, from it and from the nun. Talhah, Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read "تَرَيْنَ" (taraynā) with a sukun on the ya and a light fatha on the nun; Abu al-Fath said: "this is shadhdh (irregular)."

The meaning of this verse is that Allah the Exalted commanded her, through the tongue of Jibril or her son (peace be upon them both), as in the earlier disagreement, that she should refrain from speaking to people, and refer them to her son in that matter, so that her embarrassment would be removed and the sign would be manifest, and her excuse would stand. The apparent meaning of the verse is that she was permitted to say these words that are in the verse; this is the view of the majority. A group said: the meaning of "فَقولي" (faqūlī) is by gesture, not by speech, for otherwise the contradiction in her matter would be evident.

Ibn 'Abbas and Anas ibn Malik read: "إنِّي نَذَرْتُ لِلرَّحْمَنِ وصُمْتُ" (innī nadhartu lil-Raḥmāni wa-ṣumtu), "I have vowed to the Most Merciful and I have fasted." A people said: its meaning is a fast from speech, since the origin of fasting is abstention, and from it is the verse of the poet: "horses that abstain (ṣiyām)..." (verse continues). Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi said: the custom of fasting among them was abstaining from eating and speaking. A group read: "إنِّي نَذَرْتُ لِلرَّحْمَنِ صَمْتًا" (innī nadhartu lil-Raḥmāni ṣamtan), "I have vowed to the Most Merciful silence."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 19, verse 27–28:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him. They said, "O Maryam, you have certainly come with something monstrous.﴾ ﴿O sister of Harun, your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother a woman of unchastity."﴾

It is narrated that when Maryam (peace be upon her) was reassured by what she had seen of the sign, and knew that Allah, the Exalted, would clear her innocence, she brought him, carrying him, from the remote place to which she had withdrawn. It is narrated that her people went out seeking her and found her coming toward them. "Al-Fariyy" means the great and the abominable; this is the view of Mujahid and al-Suddi. "Iftara" means he invented it, and it derives from "al-fira" (slander). "Fara yafrih" means he split and corrupted it, and "afraa" means he set it right, from the expression "fariytu al-adim" (I cut the hide in the manner of repairing it). As for their saying in the proverb, "So-and-so does al-fariyy (the monstrous deed)," its meaning is: he has come with a great deed, whether in speech or in action, of the kind for which the proverb is coined. It is used for what is fabricated and done. "Al-fariyy" of water-skins means the new one. Abu Haywa recited "shay'an fariyyan" with the letter ra' vowelless (sukun).

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of the words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿O sister of Harun﴾. One group said: she had a brother named Harun, because this name was common among the Children of Israel, seeking blessing through the name of Harun, the brother of Musa (peace be upon them both). Al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent him to Najran on a matter of affairs, and they said: "Your companion claims that Maryam is the sister of Harun, and between them there are six hundred years." Al-Mughira said: "I did not know what to say. When I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I mentioned that to him, and he said: 'Did they not know that they used to name themselves after the prophets and the righteous?'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So the meaning is that it is a name that coincided with another name. Al-Suddi and others said: rather, they attributed her to Harun, brother of Musa, because she was of his lineage. This is like your saying of a tribe: "O brother of so-and-so," and from it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed the brother of Suda' gave the adhan, and whoever gives the adhan, he is the one who establishes the iqama." Ka'b al-Ahbar said in the presence of 'A'isha, the Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her: "She is not the sister of Harun, brother of Musa." 'A'isha said: "You have lied." He said to her: "O Mother of the Believers, if the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said it, then he is more truthful and more knowledgeable; otherwise I find between them a span of six hundred years." She said nothing. Qatada said: In that era among the Children of Israel there was a devout man, devoted wholly to Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, named Harun, so they attributed her to his brotherhood because she was upon his way. It was said: since she was dedicated to serving the churches, that is: O woman of righteousness, you were not worthy of what you brought. Another group said: rather, in that era there was a wicked man named Harun, so they attributed her to him by way of reproach and rebuke; this was mentioned by al-Tabari, who did not name its speaker. The meaning is: neither your father nor your mother was worthy of this deed, so how did you come by it? "Al-baghiyy" is the one who seeks unlawful intercourse, that is, who pursues it; its root is "baghuwy," on the pattern "fa'ul," and this has been mentioned before.

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him. They said, "O Maryam, you have certainly come with something monstrous.﴾ ﴿O sister of Harun, your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother a woman of unchastity."﴾

It is narrated that when Maryam (peace be upon her) was reassured by what she had seen of the sign, and knew that Allah, the Exalted, would clear her innocence, she brought him, carrying him, from the remote place to which she had withdrawn. It is narrated that her people went out seeking her and found her coming toward them. "Al-Fariyy" means the great and the abominable; this is the view of Mujahid and al-Suddi. "Iftara" means he invented it, and it derives from "al-fira" (slander). "Fara yafrih" means he split and corrupted it, and "afraa" means he set it right, from the expression "fariytu al-adim" (I cut the hide in the manner of repairing it). As for their saying in the proverb, "So-and-so does al-fariyy (the monstrous deed)," its meaning is: he has come with a great deed, whether in speech or in action, of the kind for which the proverb is coined. It is used for what is fabricated and done. "Al-fariyy" of water-skins means the new one. Abu Haywa recited "shay'an fariyyan" with the letter ra' vowelless (sukun).

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of the words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿O sister of Harun﴾. One group said: she had a brother named Harun, because this name was common among the Children of Israel, seeking blessing through the name of Harun, the brother of Musa (peace be upon them both). Al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent him to Najran on a matter of affairs, and they said: "Your companion claims that Maryam is the sister of Harun, and between them there are six hundred years." Al-Mughira said: "I did not know what to say. When I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I mentioned that to him, and he said: 'Did they not know that they used to name themselves after the prophets and the righteous?'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So the meaning is that it is a name that coincided with another name. Al-Suddi and others said: rather, they attributed her to Harun, brother of Musa, because she was of his lineage. This is like your saying of a tribe: "O brother of so-and-so," and from it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed the brother of Suda' gave the adhan, and whoever gives the adhan, he is the one who establishes the iqama." Ka'b al-Ahbar said in the presence of 'A'isha, the Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her: "She is not the sister of Harun, brother of Musa." 'A'isha said: "You have lied." He said to her: "O Mother of the Believers, if the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said it, then he is more truthful and more knowledgeable; otherwise I find between them a span of six hundred years." She said nothing. Qatada said: In that era among the Children of Israel there was a devout man, devoted wholly to Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, named Harun, so they attributed her to his brotherhood because she was upon his way. It was said: since she was dedicated to serving the churches, that is: O woman of righteousness, you were not worthy of what you brought. Another group said: rather, in that era there was a wicked man named Harun, so they attributed her to him by way of reproach and rebuke; this was mentioned by al-Tabari, who did not name its speaker. The meaning is: neither your father nor your mother was worthy of this deed, so how did you come by it? "Al-baghiyy" is the one who seeks unlawful intercourse, that is, who pursues it; its root is "baghuwy," on the pattern "fa'ul," and this has been mentioned before.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 19, verse 29–33:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿So she pointed to him. They said, "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a young child?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet.﴾ ﴿And He has made me blessed wherever I am, and has enjoined upon me prayer and zakah as long as I remain alive,﴾ ﴿and [made me] dutiful to my mother, and He has not made me a wretched tyrant.﴾ ﴿And peace is upon me the day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised alive.﴾

Maryam, peace be upon her, adhered to what she had been commanded regarding abstaining from speech. This verse does not report that she spoke the words ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾ [Maryam: 26]; rather, it reports only that she gestured. This strengthens the view of those who said that her command in ﴿So say﴾ was intended to mean gesturing. It is also related that when she pointed to the infant, they said: "Her mocking us is more grievous to us than her fornication." Then they said to her, in the manner of a rebuke, ﴿How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a young child?﴾

The word "kāna" here is not intended to denote the past, because each one of us was once in the cradle as a young child; rather, it carries the meaning of "is" (now). It may be the defective (nāqisa) verb, but the more evident reading is that it is the complete (tāmma) verb. Abu 'Ubayda said: "kāna" here is superfluous (laghw). Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: "man" in His saying, blessed and exalted, ﴿man kāna﴾ is conditional.

(p-29)The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

A parallel to this "kāna" is the verse of Ru'ba:

"And the head had, for it, a [grey] hair"

"Ṣabiyyan" is either the predicate of "kāna" by way of metaphor and imagination if it is taken as defective, or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) [if it is taken as redundant or complete], due to the stability of what is implied in the sentence.

It is related that "al-mahd" is meant to be the lap of his mother. Speaking to them from his cradle, 'Isa said: "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah," to the end of the verse. It is also related that he rose up leaning on his left side and pointed to them with his right index finger. "Al-Kitab" is the Torah; it is also possible that it means the Torah and the Gospel. "Ataniya" means: He decreed this and executed it in His prior decree. This is similar to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1], and other than this. Al-Kisa'i pronounced "ataniya" and "awsaniya" with imala, while the rest did not use imala. Abu 'Ali said: imala in "ataniya" is better, not in "awsaniya."

"Mubarakan": Mujahid said its meaning is "beneficial" (naffa'an). Sufyan al-Thawri said its meaning is "a teacher of good." (p-30) It was also said: "commanding what is good and forbidding what is evil." A man said to one of the scholars: "What is the knowledge I should make public?" He said: "Enjoining good and forbidding evil, for it is the religion of Allah with which He sent His prophets." Al-Naqqash transmitted from al-Dahhak that he said: "Mubarakan" means "one who fulfils needs."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

His saying, Exalted is He, "mubarakan," encompasses these meanings and others.

"Al-salat wa al-zakat": it was said these are the two obligations regarding the body and wealth; it was said that the zakat is the zakat of heads at the end of Ramadan (zakat al-fitr); it was said that salat is supplication and zakat is purification from every defect, deficiency and disobedience. ﴿Dumtu﴾ was read with a damma on the dal by 'Asim and a group, and read with a kasra by the people of Madina, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and a group.

The majority read "wa-barran" with a fatha on the ba' — meaning one who is abundantly dutiful — and in the accusative by virtue of its being parallel to "mubarakan." Abu Nahik, Abu Mijlaz and a group read "birran" with a kasra on the ba'. Some said its accusative is by coordination with "mubarakan," as if he said: "possessing dutifulness," so he was described by the verbal noun, like "'adl" and similar. Others said its accusative is governed by His saying "wa-awsani," meaning: "and He enjoined upon me dutifulness to my mother," the preposition having been omitted, intending: "and He enjoined upon me the dutifulness of my mother." Al-Zahrawi transmitted the reading "wa-birrin" with a genitive, coordinated with "al-zakat." His saying "bi-walidati" is an explanation, since he had no father; and by this statement his people were cleared of accusation.

"Al-jabbar" is the one who magnifies himself. It is a trait associated with wretchedness, because it contradicts all people, so its possessor meets with nothing from anyone but what is disliked. 'Isa, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, was in the utmost humility: he would eat plants, wear wool, sit on the earth, and lodge wherever night overtook him, having no dwelling. Qatada said: he would say, "Ask me, for I am gentle of heart and humble in myself." His greeting of peace upon himself and his appeal in that have already been mentioned, along with the occasions he specified, because they are the times when a person most needs the mercy of Allah.

(p-31) Malik ibn Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said regarding this verse: "How severe it is against the people of qadar! 'Isa informed of what had been decreed concerning his affair and what would occur until he died." It is related in the narratives on this verse from Ibn Zayd and others that when they heard the speech of 'Isa while he was in the cradle, they submitted and said: "Indeed, this is a great matter." It is also related that 'Isa, peace be upon him, spoke in his childhood only with this verse, then returned to the state of infants until he grew up in the customary manner of humans. A group said: 'Isa had been given the Scripture (al-kuttab) at that age, and he would fast and pray.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is extremely weak, and it plainly reveals the ignorance of its proponent.
