It is also related that 'Isa, peace be upon him, spoke in his childhood only with this verse, then returned to the state of infants until he grew up in the customary manner of humans. A group said: 'Isa had been given the Scripture (al-kuttab) at that age, and he would fast and pray.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is extremely weak, and it plainly reveals the ignorance of its proponent.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 19, verse 29–33:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿So she pointed to him. They said, "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a young child?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet.﴾ ﴿And He has made me blessed wherever I am, and has enjoined upon me prayer and zakah as long as I remain alive,﴾ ﴿and [made me] dutiful to my mother, and He has not made me a wretched tyrant.﴾ ﴿And peace is upon me the day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised alive.﴾

Maryam, peace be upon her, adhered to what she had been commanded regarding abstaining from speech. This verse does not report that she spoke the words ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾ [Maryam: 26]; rather, it reports only that she gestured. This strengthens the view of those who said that her command in ﴿So say﴾ was intended to mean gesturing. It is also related that when she pointed to the infant, they said: "Her mocking us is more grievous to us than her fornication." Then they said to her, in the manner of a rebuke, ﴿How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a young child?﴾

The word "kāna" here is not intended to denote the past, because each one of us was once in the cradle as a young child; rather, it carries the meaning of "is" (now). It may be the defective (nāqisa) verb, but the more evident reading is that it is the complete (tāmma) verb. Abu 'Ubayda said: "kāna" here is superfluous (laghw). Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: "man" in His saying, blessed and exalted, ﴿man kāna﴾ is conditional.

(p-29)The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

A parallel to this "kāna" is the verse of Ru'ba:

"And the head had, for it, a [grey] hair"

"Ṣabiyyan" is either the predicate of "kāna" by way of metaphor and imagination if it is taken as defective, or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) [if it is taken as redundant or complete], due to the stability of what is implied in the sentence.

It is related that "al-mahd" is meant to be the lap of his mother. Speaking to them from his cradle, 'Isa said: "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah," to the end of the verse. It is also related that he rose up leaning on his left side and pointed to them with his right index finger. "Al-Kitab" is the Torah; it is also possible that it means the Torah and the Gospel. "Ataniya" means: He decreed this and executed it in His prior decree. This is similar to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1], and other than this. Al-Kisa'i pronounced "ataniya" and "awsaniya" with imala, while the rest did not use imala. Abu 'Ali said: imala in "ataniya" is better, not in "awsaniya."

"Mubarakan": Mujahid said its meaning is "beneficial" (naffa'an). Sufyan al-Thawri said its meaning is "a teacher of good." (p-30) It was also said: "commanding what is good and forbidding what is evil." A man said to one of the scholars: "What is the knowledge I should make public?" He said: "Enjoining good and forbidding evil, for it is the religion of Allah with which He sent His prophets." Al-Naqqash transmitted from al-Dahhak that he said: "Mubarakan" means "one who fulfils needs."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

His saying, Exalted is He, "mubarakan," encompasses these meanings and others.

"Al-salat wa al-zakat": it was said these are the two obligations regarding the body and wealth; it was said that the zakat is the zakat of heads at the end of Ramadan (zakat al-fitr); it was said that salat is supplication and zakat is purification from every defect, deficiency and disobedience. ﴿Dumtu﴾ was read with a damma on the dal by 'Asim and a group, and read with a kasra by the people of Madina, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and a group.

The majority read "wa-barran" with a fatha on the ba' — meaning one who is abundantly dutiful — and in the accusative by virtue of its being parallel to "mubarakan." Abu Nahik, Abu Mijlaz and a group read "birran" with a kasra on the ba'. Some said its accusative is by coordination with "mubarakan," as if he said: "possessing dutifulness," so he was described by the verbal noun, like "'adl" and similar. Others said its accusative is governed by His saying "wa-awsani," meaning: "and He enjoined upon me dutifulness to my mother," the preposition having been omitted, intending: "and He enjoined upon me the dutifulness of my mother." Al-Zahrawi transmitted the reading "wa-birrin" with a genitive, coordinated with "al-zakat." His saying "bi-walidati" is an explanation, since he had no father; and by this statement his people were cleared of accusation.

"Al-jabbar" is the one who magnifies himself. It is a trait associated with wretchedness, because it contradicts all people, so its possessor meets with nothing from anyone but what is disliked. 'Isa, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, was in the utmost humility: he would eat plants, wear wool, sit on the earth, and lodge wherever night overtook him, having no dwelling. Qatada said: he would say, "Ask me, for I am gentle of heart and humble in myself." His greeting of peace upon himself and his appeal in that have already been mentioned, along with the occasions he specified, because they are the times when a person most needs the mercy of Allah.

(p-31) Malik ibn Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said regarding this verse: "How severe it is against the people of qadar! 'Isa informed of what had been decreed concerning his affair and what would occur until he died." It is related in the narratives on this verse from Ibn Zayd and others that when they heard the speech of 'Isa while he was in the cradle, they submitted and said: "Indeed, this is a great matter." It is also related that 'Isa, peace be upon him, spoke in his childhood only with this verse, then returned to the state of infants until he grew up in the customary manner of humans. A group said: 'Isa had been given the Scripture (al-kuttab) at that age, and he would fast and pray.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is extremely weak, and it plainly reveals the ignorance of its proponent.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 19, verses 34–36:

His the Exalted's saying:

﴿That is Jesus, son of Mary, a statement of truth about which they dispute.﴾ ﴿It is not for Allah to take a son; glory be to Him. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.﴾

The meaning: Say, O Muhammad, to your contemporaries among the Jews and Christians: "That is the account of Jesus, son of Mary."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

We supposed "say" (qul) in the wording because it comes in the verse after "Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord," and this is the statement of a human being. The apparent meaning of the verse does not require any speaker among humans other than Muhammad ﷺ. It is possible that his saying "That is Jesus" up to his saying "and it is" is an informing address to Muhammad ﷺ and an interjection within the speech of Jesus, and that his saying "wa-anna" with the alif opened is a conjunction with his saying "the Book." Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Jesus charged them that "Allah is my Lord and your Lord." Whoever reads the alif with a kasra connects it to his saying "Indeed I am the servant of Allah."

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Hamza, al-Kisa'i and the general body of readers recite "qawlu al-haqq" (with a damma), while 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Ibn Abi Ishaq recite "qawla al-haqq" with a fatha on "al-qawl" as a verbal noun (masdar). Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Muqri said: A trustworthy blind man used to sit with me and said: "I saw the Prophet ﷺ in a dream reciting 'qawla al-haqq' with a fatha." Abu 'Abd al-Rahman said: I used to recite only with the damma, so I began reciting both. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud recited "qala Allah," meaning: the word of Allah. 'Isa recited "qala al-haqqa."

Nafi' and the majority recite "yamtarun" with the ya', as a reference to them (third person). Nafi' also, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Dawud ibn Abi Hind recite "tamtarun" with the ta', as addressing them directly. The meaning is: you disagree, O Jews and Christians, so some of them say he was born of fornication and the like, and some say he is Allah, the Exalted. This is their disputing, and its explanation will come later.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿It is not for Allah to take a son; glory be to Him.﴾ Its meaning is negation, and this is the meaning of these expressions wherever they occur. Then something is added to it according to the context of what is mentioned in them: either a rebuke and prohibition, as in His saying: ﴿It was not for the people of Medina and those of the Bedouins around them to remain behind﴾ [al-Tawbah: 120], or an declaration of incapacity, as in His saying: ﴿It was not for you to grow its trees﴾ [al-Naml: 60], or a declaration of His freedom from it, as in this verse. As for His saying "min walad" (a son), the particle "min" has entered as an emphasis of the negation, to negate one and what is above it of what could be conceived, and the equivalent of this phrasing when "min" does not enter is similar. As for His saying "amran" (a matter), it means one of the matters, and it is not the verbal noun of "amara ya'muru." Thus the meaning of "qada" is: He brought into existence and brought out from non-existence. These variations of tense in these verbs, past and future, are according to the Arabs' figurative usage and its breadth. The discussion of His saying "Be, and it is" has already preceded.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr recite "wa-anna Allah" with the alif opened, which is a conjunction with His saying: ﴿That is Jesus, son of Mary, a statement of truth﴾ and ﴿Indeed, Allah is my Lord﴾, in the same way. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recite "wa-inna Allah" with the alif kasra, and that is clear as a fresh resumption of speech. Ubayy ibn Ka'b (may Allah be pleased with him) recited "inna Allah rabbi wa-rabbukum" with the alif kasra and without the waw.

His saying: ﴿so worship Him﴾, one pauses, then begins: ﴿This is a straight path﴾, meaning: what I have informed you of from Allah, the Exalted, regarding His oneness, the negation of a son from Him, and other things from which He is far removed, is a clear path leading to salvation and the mercy of Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 19, verses 37–40:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿But the factions differed among themselves, so woe to those who disbelieve, from the scene of a tremendous Day.﴾ ﴿How well they will hear and see on the Day they come to Us! But the wrongdoers today are in clear error.﴾ ﴿And warn them of the Day of regret, when the matter will be decided, while they are in heedlessness and do not believe.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We inherit the earth and whoever is upon it, and to Us they will be returned.﴾

This is the beginning of a report from Allah, Exalted and Majestic, to Muhammad (ﷺ) that the Children of Israel differed into factions (aḥzāban), i.e., sects (firaq). His saying ﴿from among themselves﴾ means that the difference did not come from outside them; rather, they were the ones who differed. It is narrated on this authority from Qatada that the Children of Israel gathered four rabbis from among themselves, who held the highest rank and dignity among them, and they asked them to explain the matter of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. One of them said: "ʿĪsā is Allah; he descended to the earth, gave life to whomever he gave life, caused death, and then ascended." The other three said to him: "You have lied." His followers were the Yaʿqūbiyya. Then it was said to the three, and one of them said: "ʿĪsā is the son of Allah." The other two said to him: "You have lied." His followers were the Nasṭūriyya. Then it was said to the two, and one of them said: "ʿĪsā is one of three; ʿĪsā is God, Maryam is God, and Allah is God." The fourth said to him: "You have lied." His followers were the Isrāʾīliyya. Then it was said to the fourth, and he said: "ʿĪsā is the Spirit of Allah and His Word, which He cast to Maryam." So a group of the Children of Israel followed each of the four, and then they fought one another; the believers were overcome and killed, and the Yaʿqūbiyya prevailed over all.

It is also narrated that concerning this the following was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right, and kill those among people who enjoin justice — give them the tidings of a painful punishment.﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 21].

And "al-Waylu" (woe): grief and destruction. It is said: "Waylun" is a valley in Hell. "The scene of a tremendous Day" is the scene of the Day of Resurrection. It is possible that what is meant by ﴿the scene of a tremendous Day﴾ is the day on which the believers were killed when the factions differed; Qatada, may Allah have mercy on him, pointed to this meaning.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿How well they will hear and see﴾, meaning: how much they will hear and see on the day they return to Us and witness what We do to them of punishment, for their aversion will then vanish and they will turn toward the truth at a time when turning toward it will not benefit them, whereas in the world they were deaf, dumb and blind, since looking will not benefit them while they are averse. Then He said: "But the wrongdoers today are in clear error in the world," and "error" means ignorance of the path. And "al-Mubīn" (clear): clear in itself, even if it has not been made clear to them. Al-Ṭabarī narrated from Abū al-ʿĀliya that he said: "How well they will hear and see" is in the form of a command to Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: make the people hear and see today through them and their speech, what punishment is being done to them when they come gathered and defeated.

Scholars differed concerning ﴿the Day of regret﴾. The majority said: it is the day of the slaughter of Death. In this there is a sound ḥadīth recorded in al-Bukhārī and others: "Death will be brought in the form of a white-speckled ram," and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr said: "as if it were an animal," "and it will be slaughtered on the Ṣirāṭ between Paradise and the Fire, and it will be proclaimed: O people of Paradise, eternity without death; and O people of the Fire, eternity without death." It is also reported that the people of the Fire will strain their necks toward it, hoping to leave what they are in, and the people of Paradise will strain their necks out of fear for what they are in. "The decreed matter" is the slaughter of the ram, which is the example of death. This, according to the discerning scholars, is like saying: (p-35) "the calamities are buried, and dust is placed under the foot," and similar. At that point a regret will strike the people of the Fire such that there is no regret like it.

Ibn Zayd and others said: the Day of regret is the Day of Resurrection, because the people of the Fire had, from the very beginning of their affair, incurred the wrath and sign of Allah, so they are in a state of regret. The "decreed matter," on this view, is the certain sentence of punishment upon them and the manifestation of its execution upon them. Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the Day of regret is when the disbelievers see their seats in Paradise that they missed, had they been believers.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that "the Day of regret" is a generic noun, because these are many regrets in several situations, among them the Day of Resurrection, among them the time when the book is taken in the left hand, and other things.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿while they are in heedlessness﴾ means: in the world, now, and they do not believe in that manner.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We inherit the earth﴾ is a figurative expression and an idiom for the passing away of created things and the remaining of the Creator, so it is as if it were an inheritance. ʿĀṣim, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿmash read "yurjaʿūn" with the yāʾ; al-Aʿraj read "turjaʿūn" with the tāʾ from above; Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Ibn Abī Isḥāq and ʿĪsā read "yarjiʿūn" with the yāʾ fatḥa and kasra on the jīm; and Abū ʿAmr related from them "tarjiʿūn" with the tāʾ.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 19, verse 41–46:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And mention in the Book Abraham. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet.﴾ ﴿When he said to his father, "O my father, why do you worship that which does not hear and does not see and will not benefit you at all?"﴾ ﴿"O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to a straight path.﴾ ﴿"O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, Satan has been, to the Most Merciful, disobedient.﴾ ﴿"O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you would be to Satan a companion."﴾ ﴿He said, "Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham? If you do not desist, I will surely stone you, so leave me alone for a long time."﴾

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And mention﴾ means: recite and convey, because Allah, the Exalted, is the One who mentions. "The Book" is the Qur'an. This is what resembles the tongue of truth which Allah left for them. "Ṣiddīq" (one who is exceedingly truthful) is on the pattern of fa'īl, a form of intensification from ṣidq (truthfulness). Abu al-Barahsam recited: "Innahu kāna ṣādiqan" (indeed he was truthful). The common usage of ṣidq in speech is consistent in actions and creation, except that it is borrowed for what does not reason, so it is said: "The food truly (ṣadaqanī) such-and-such a qafīz," and it is said: "a true wood (ʿawd ṣidq)" for the sound, good tree trunk.

Abraham, peace be upon him, was described as truthful in general in his sayings and actions, and this encompasses truthfulness of tongue, which is opposed to lying. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, was described as ṣiddīq because of his abundant truthfulness in affirming the realities, and his truthfulness in hastening to faith and what brings one closer to Allah, blessed and exalted. There are degrees of ṣiddīq; do you not see that the believers are ṣiddīqūn, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who believed in Allah and His messengers—they are the ṣiddīqūn﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 19].

And His saying: ﴿O my father﴾. The grammarians differed concerning the tā' in "abatī" (ābatī): the position of Sibawayh is that it is a substitute for the yā' of possession, and it is pausing on it with a hā'; the position of al-Farrā' is that one pauses on it with a tā', because the yā' of possession is, in his view, intended (implied). The majority of reciters read it with a kasra on the tā'. In the Muṣḥaf of Ibn Mas'ud it is "Wa abatī" with a wāw for the vocative. Ibn 'Āmir, al-A'raj, and Abu Ja'far read "Yā abatā" with a fatḥa on the tā'; its explanation is that he intended "yā abatā," so he deleted the alif and left the fatḥa indicating it. Another explanation is that the inserted tā' is like that in their saying "yā Ṭalḥatu aqbil." In this there is consideration, and Hārūn declared this reading to be a solecism.

"The one who does not hear and does not see" is the idol. Had it heard and seen, as is the state of the angels and others who are worshipped, its worship would not have been good; but Abraham, peace be upon him, by negating hearing and sight, made clear the ugliness of the opinion regarding its worship and its corruption.

His saying: ﴿There has come to me﴾ indicates that this dialogue took place after he had been given prophethood. The "straight path" (al-ṣirāṭ al-sawiyy) means: the straight road, and it is the path of faith.

His saying: ﴿O my father, do not worship Satan﴾ is an address of kindness and gentle appeal regarding his state of disbelief. His saying: ﴿Do not worship Satan﴾ may mean that his father was among those who worshipped the jinn, and it may mean that obedience to the figurative Satan in worshipping idols and disbelieving in Allah is considered worship of him. "ʿAṣiyy" is on the pattern of fa'īl from ʿaṣā, yaʿṣī, when one opposes a command.

His saying: ﴿Indeed I fear﴾: al-Ṭabarī and others said: "akhāfu" means: "aʿlamu" (I know).

The qāḍī Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning to me is that it is fear in its proper sense; that is because Abraham, peace be upon him, was not, at the time of this dialogue, despairing of his father, so he was hoping for that, and he feared that he would not believe and would persist in his disbelief until death, whereupon the punishment would touch him. "Walī": the sincere companion, close by lineage or affection.

Āzar, who is Tārakh, said: ﴿Do you turn away from my gods?﴾ Ar-raghbah is the inclination of the soul; one may have desire for a thing, and one may have aversion from it. His saying: ﴿Do you turn away?﴾ (a-rāghibun) is raised as the subject of the inchoative, and "anta" is the agent that fills the place of the predicate; what made this acceptable and brought it near is the reliance of "rāghib" upon the alif of interrogation. It is permissible that "rāghib" be a fronted predicate and "anta" the subject, but the first is more correct, and it is the position of Sibawayh. His saying: ﴿from my gods﴾ means the idols; it is reported that he used to carve them, fashion them with his hand, sell them, and urge people toward them. So his son Abraham, peace be upon him, affirmed his aversion from them in the form of rebuke to him, then began to threaten him.

His saying: ﴿I will surely stone you﴾ has been differed over by the interpreters. al-Suddī, Ibn Jurayj, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: its meaning is "with speech," i.e., "I will surely revile you; so leave me alone, you, if you wish, for a period of time, or safely," according to the difference which we shall mention. al-Ḥasan ibn Abi al-Ḥasan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: its meaning is "I will surely stone you with stones." A group said: its meaning is "I will surely kill you."

These two statements have one meaning. His saying: ﴿And leave me﴾, on this interpretation, is only consequent upon his having commanded him during his life; as if he said: "If you do not desist, I will kill you by stoning," then he said to him: "and leave me," i.e., together with your desisting, as if he decisively commanded him to migrate; otherwise, with stoning, migration would not follow. "Maliyy" (for a long time) means a long age, derived from al-malawayn, which are the night and the day. This is the saying of the majority, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and others, so it is an adverb of time.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Maliyy" means: safe, sound, so it is a circumstantial state of [Abraham], peace be upon him.

The qāḍī Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The summary of this is that it has the meaning of his saying: "independent of your state from me, wealthy, sufficient in self-reliance."

His saying: ﴿Indeed I fear﴾: al-Ṭabarī and others said: "akhāfu" means: "aʿlamu" (I know).

The qāḍī Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning to me is that it is fear in its proper sense; that is because Abraham, peace be upon him, was not, at the time of this dialogue, despairing of his father, so he was hoping for that, and he feared that he would not believe and would persist in his disbelief until death, whereupon the punishment would touch him. "Walī": the sincere companion, close by lineage or affection.

Āzar, who is Tārakh, said: ﴿Do you turn away from my gods?﴾ Ar-raghbah is the inclination of the soul; one may have desire for a thing, and one may have aversion from it. His saying: ﴿Do you turn away?﴾ (a-rāghibun) is raised as the subject of the inchoative, and "anta" is the agent that fills the place of the predicate; what made this acceptable and brought it near is the reliance of "rāghib" upon the alif of interrogation. It is permissible that "rāghib" be a fronted predicate and "anta" the subject, but the first is more correct, and it is the position of Sibawayh. His saying: ﴿from my gods﴾ means the idols; it is reported that he used to carve them, fashion them with his hand, sell them, and urge people toward them. So his son Abraham, peace be upon him, affirmed his aversion from them in the form of rebuke to him, then began to threaten him.

His saying: ﴿I will surely stone you﴾ has been differed over by the interpreters. al-Suddī, Ibn Jurayj, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: its meaning is "with speech," i.e., "I will surely revile you; so leave me alone, you, if you wish, for a period of time, or safely," according to the difference which we shall mention. al-Ḥasan ibn Abi al-Ḥasan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: its meaning is "I will surely stone you with stones." A group said: its meaning is "I will surely kill you."

These two statements have one meaning. His saying: ﴿And leave me﴾, on this interpretation, is only consequent upon his having commanded him during his life; as if he said: "If you do not desist, I will kill you by stoning," then he said to him: "and leave me," i.e., together with your desisting, as if he decisively commanded him to migrate; otherwise, with stoning, migration would not follow. "Maliyy" (for a long time) means a long age, derived from al-malawayn, which are the night and the day. This is the saying of the majority, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and others, so it is an adverb of time.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Maliyy" means: safe, sound, so it is a circumstantial state of [Abraham], peace be upon him.

The qāḍī Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The summary of this is that it has the meaning of his saying: "independent of your state from me, wealthy, sufficient in self-reliance."

﴿He said, "Peace be upon you. I will ask my Lord to forgive you, for He has always been gracious to me. قَرَأ أبُو البَرَهْسَمِ: "سَلامًا" بِالنَصْبِ. واخْتَلَفَ أهْلُ العِلْمِ في مَعْنى تَسْلِيمِهِ عَلَيْهِ - فَقالَ بَعْضُهُمْ: هي تَحِيَّةُ مُفارِقٍ، وجَوَّزُوا تَحِيَّةَ الكافِرِ، وأنْ يُبْدَأ بِها، وقالَ الجُمْهُورُ: ذَلِكَ التَسْلِيمُ بِمَعْنى المُسالَمَةِ لا بِمَعْنى التَحِيَّةِ، قالَ الطَبَرِيُّ: مَعْناهُ: أمَنَةٌ مِنِّي لَكَ، وهَذا قَوْلُ الجُمْهُورِ، وهم لا يَرَوْنَ ابْتِداءَ الكافِرِ بِالسَلامِ. وقالَ النَقّاشُ: حَلِيمٌ خاطَبَ سَفِيهًا، كَما قالَ تَعالى: ﴿وَإذا خاطَبَهُمُ الجاهِلُونَ قالُوا سَلامًا﴾ [الفرقان: ٦٣]، ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾ ورَفْعَ "السَلامُ" بِالِابْتِداءِ، وجازَ ذَلِكَ مَعَ كَوْنِهِ نَكِرَةً مُخَصَّصَةً، فَقَرُبَتْ مِنَ المَعْرِفَةِ، ولِأنَّهُ في مَوْضِعِ المَنصُوبِ الَّذِي هُوَ: سَلَّمْتَ سَلامًا، وهَذا كَما يَجُوزُ ذَلِكَ فِيما هو في مَعْنى الفاعِلِ، كَقَوْلِهِمْ: "شَرٌّ أهَرَّ ذا نابٌ"، هَذا مَقالُ سِيبَوَيْهِ رَحِمَهُ اللهُ.

(p-٣٩)وَقَوْلُهُ: ﴿سَأسْتَغْفِرُ﴾ مَعْناهُ: سَأدْعُو اللهَ تَعالى في أنْ يَهْدِيَكَ، فَيَغْفِرُ لَكَ بِإيمانِكَ.

قالَ القاضِي أبُو مُحَمَّدٍ رَحِمَهُ اللهُ:

وهَذا أظْهَرُ مِن أنْ يُتَأوَّلَ عَلى إبْراهِيمَ الخَلِيلِ صَلَواتُ اللهِ عَلَيْهِ أنَّهُ لَمْ يَعْلَمْ أنَّ اللهَ تَعالى لا يَغْفِرُ لِكافِرٍ، وقَدْ يَجُوزُ أنْ يَكُونَ إبْراهِيمُ عَلَيْهِ السَلامُ أوَّلَ نَبِيٍّ أُوحِيَ إلَيْهِ أنْ لا يُغْفَرُ لِكافِرٍ؛ لِأنَّ هَذِهِ العَقِيدَةَ إنَّما طَرِيقُها السَمْعُ، فَكانَتْ هَذِهِ المَقالَةُ مِنهُ لِأبِيهِ قَبْلَ أنْ يُوحى إلَيْهِ ذَلِكَ، وإبْراهِيمُ عَلَيْهِ السَلامُ إنَّما تَبَيَّنَ لَهُ في أبِيهِ أنَّهُ عَدُوٌّ لِلَّهِ بِأحَدِ وجْهَيْنِ: إمّا بِمَوْتِهِ عَلى الكُفْرِ كَما رُوِيَ، وإمّا بِأنْ أُوحِيَ إلَيْهِ تَعَسُّفُ الحَتْمِ عَلَيْهِ. وقالَ مَكِّيٌّ عَنِ السُدِّيِّ: أخَّرَهُ بِالِاسْتِغْفارِ إلى السَحَرِ.

وقَوْلُهُ: ﴿فَلَمّا اعْتَزَلَهم وما يَعْبُدُونَ مِن دُونِ اللهِ﴾ الآيَةُ إخْبارٌ مِنَ اللهِ تَبارَكَ وتَعالى لِمُحَمَّدٍ (ﷺ) أنَّ إبْراهِيمَ عَلَيْهِ السَلامُ لَمّا رَحَلَ عن بَلَدِ أبِيهِ وبَلَدِ قَوْمِهِ عَوَّضَهُ اللهُ مِن ذَلِكَ ابْنَهُ إسْحاقَ وابْنَ ابْنِهِ يَعْقُوبَ عَلَيْهِما السَلامُ، وجُعِلَ لَهُ الوَلَدُ تَسْلِيَةً وشَدًّا لِعَضُدِهِ، وإسْحاقُ أصْغَرُ مِن إسْماعِيلَ ؛ ولَمّا حَمَلَتْ هاجَرُ بِإسْماعِيلَ غارَتْ سارَّةُ فَحَمَلَتْ بِإسْحاقَ فِيما رُوِيَ.

؎ إنِّي أتَتْنِي لِسانٌ لا أُسِرُّ بِها مِن عُلُوٍّ لا كَذِبَ فِيها ولا سَخِرَ

؎ "Indeed a tongue has come to me, which I do not keep secret, from on high, in which there is no lie and no mockery."

وقالَ آخَرٌ:

؎ نَدِمْتُ عَلى لِسانٍ فاتَ مِنِّي ∗∗∗..............

؎ "I regretted a tongue that escaped from me..." ∗∗∗..............

قالَ القاضِي أبُو مُحَمَّدٍ رَحِمَهُ اللهُ:

وهَذا تَعَسُّفٌ، وإنَّما ذُكِرَ ذَلِكَ في أمْرِ يَعْقُوبَ وبَنِيهِ، وأمّا هَذا فَوَعْدٌ بِاسْتِغْفارٍ كَثِيرٍ مُؤْتَنِفٍ، فالسِينُ مُتَمَكِّنَةٌ.

و"الحَفِيُّ": المُبْتَهِلُ المُتَلَطِّفُ، وهَذا شُكْرٌ مِن إبْراهِيمَ عَلَيْهِ السَلامُ لِنِعَمِ اللهِ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ. ثُمْ أخْبَرَهُ أنَّهُ يَعْتَزِلُهُمْ، أيْ: يَصِيرُ عنهم بِمَعْزِلٍ، ويُرْوى أنَّهم كانُوا بِأرْضِ كَوْثى، فانْتَقَلَ إبْراهِيمُ عَلَيْهِ السَلامُ إلى الشامِ، وفي هِجْرَتِهِ تِلْكَ لَقِيَ الجَبّارُ الَّذِي أخْدَمَ هاجَرَ بِسارَّةَ.... الحَدِيثُ بِطُولِهِ. و"تَدْعُونَ": تَعْبُدُونَ. وقَوْلُهُ: "عَسى" تَرَجٍّ وفي ضِمْنِهِ خَوْفٌ شَدِيدٌ.

(p-٤٠)قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَوَهَبْنا لَهم مِن رَحْمَتِنا﴾ يُرِيدُ العِلْمَ والمَنزِلَةَ والشَرَفَ في الدُنْيا والنَعِيمَ في الآخِرَةِ، كُلُّ ذَلِكَ مِن رَحْمَةِ اللهِ، و"لِسانُ الصِدْقِ" هو الثَناءُ الباقِي عَلَيْهِمْ آخِرَ الأبَدِ، قالَهُ عَبْدُ اللهِ بْنُ عَبّاسٍ رَضِيَ اللهُ عنهُما. واللِسانُ في كَلامِ العَرَبِ المَقالَةُ الذائِعَةُ كانَتْ في خَيْرٍ أو شَرٍّ، ومِنهُ قَوْلُ الشاعِرِ:

؎ إنِّي أتَتْنِي لِسانٌ لا أُسِرُّ بِها مِن عُلُوٍّ لا كَذِبَ فِيها ولا سَخِرَ

؎ "Indeed a tongue has come to me, which I do not keep secret, from on high, in which there is no lie and no mockery."

وقالَ آخَرٌ:

؎ نَدِمْتُ عَلى لِسانٍ فاتَ مِنِّي ∗∗∗..............

؎ "I regretted a tongue that escaped from me..." ∗∗∗..............

وإبْراهِيمُ عَلَيْهِ السَلامُ - وذُرِّيَّتُهُ - مُعَظَّمٌ في جَمِيعِ الأُمَمِ والمَمالِكِ، صَلّى اللهُ عَلَيْهِمْ أجْمَعِينَ.

(p-٤١)

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 19, verse 51–55:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And mention in the Book Moses; indeed, he was chosen, and he was a messenger and a prophet.﴾ ﴿And We called him from the right side of the mountain and brought him near in confidence.﴾ ﴿And We gave him, out of Our mercy, his brother Aaron as a prophet.﴾ ﴿And mention in the Book Ishmael; indeed, he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet.﴾ ﴿And he used to enjoin on his people prayer and zakah, and he was pleasing to his Lord.﴾

This is a command from Allah, Exalted and Majestic, to mention Moses son of 'Imran, upon him be the blessings of Allah, in a manner of honour. He informed us that he was "mukhlasan" (chosen/purified). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "mukhlisan" with a kasra on the lam, which is the reading of the majority, meaning: he sincerely devoted himself to Allah, Exalted is He. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read "mukhlasan" with a fatha on the lam, which is the reading of Abu Razin, Yahya and Qatadah, meaning: Allah, Exalted is He, chose him for prophethood and leadership, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We chose them with a pure quality﴾ [Sad: 46]. And "rasul" (messenger) among the prophets is the one who is charged with conveying to his community; and one may be a prophet without being a messenger.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We called him from the right side of the mountain﴾ refers to Allah's speaking to Moses, peace be upon him. "al-Tur" (the mountain) is the well-known mountain in al-Sham. His saying "al-Ayman" (the right) is an attribute of "al-janib" (the side), and it was on Moses' right when he stood there; otherwise the mountain itself has no right or left, and it is not described by any of that except by being related to one who has a right and a left.

It is possible that "al-Ayman" is derived from "al-yumn" (blessing), as if he said: the most blessed and most fortunate, and on this view it is correct that it is an attribute of the side and of the mountain as a whole. His saying: ﴿And We brought him near in confidence﴾ refers to bringing him close by honouring him with speech and prophethood. 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: rather, Moses was brought close to the malakut, and the veils were lifted for him until he heard the scratching of the pens. Maysarah, may Allah have mercy on him, also said this. Sa'id said: Jibril, upon him be peace, rode behind him. As for "al-najiy" (confidant), it was said: it is from "munajah," which is speaking in a low voice secretly. Qatadah said: its meaning is: he was saved by charity.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is unsound; rather "al-najiy" is the one who is alone in private conversation. Harun was older than Moses, peace be upon them both, so he (Moses) asked Allah to strengthen his back with his prophethood and support, and Allah granted him that, and counted it among His blessings upon him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And mention in the Book Ishmael; indeed, he was true to his promise﴾ is likewise from the tongue of truthfulness and honour whose continuance is guaranteed upon the family of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. Ishmael, peace be upon him, is the father of the Arabs today, since the Yemenite and the Mudarite lineages trace back to the sons of Ishmael, peace be upon him. He is the one whom his father settled in a valley without cultivation, and he is the sacrificed one according to the majority's view, while a group said the sacrificed one is Isaac, peace be upon him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first view is preferred for several reasons. Among them is Allah's saying: ﴿And after Isaac, Jacob﴾ [Hud: 71]; so a son whose parents were given glad tidings that a son would come from him, who is a grandson to them, how would he then be commanded to slaughter him, when this promise had already preceded? Another aspect is that there is no disagreement among the scholars that the command of the sacrifice took place at Mina near Makkah, and it was never narrated that Isaac entered that land, whereas Ishmael grew up there; and his father used to visit many times, coming from al-Sham on the Buraq and returning the same day, and the Buraq is the mount of the prophets, peace be upon them. Another aspect is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "I am the son of the two sacrificed ones," the first being his father 'Abdullah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, since he was ransomed with camels from being slaughtered, and the second sacrificed one is his forefather Ishmael, peace be upon him. Another aspect is the verses in Surat al-Saffat, for when He had finished mentioning the sacrifice and its circumstances, He said: ﴿And We gave him glad tidings of Isaac﴾ [al-Saffat: 112]; so the arrangement of those verses nearly makes explicit that the sacrificed one is other than Isaac, peace be upon him.

Allah, Exalted is He, described Ishmael with truthfulness of promise because he was exceptionally so in this. It is narrated that he promised a man to meet him at a certain place, and Ishmael, peace be upon him, came and waited for the man for his whole day and night; when the next day came, the man arrived and said to him: "I have been here waiting for you since yesterday." And in the book of Ibn Salam it is said that he waited for him for a year.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is distant and not sound; the first (account) is more correct. Our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ did the like before his mission, as al-Naqqash mentioned, and al-Tirmidhi and others transmitted it, and that was in a transaction and trade. It was also said: He described him with truthfulness of promise for his fulfilment of himself in the matter of the sacrifice, when he said: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast﴾ [al-Saffat: 102]. Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the worst lying is breaking a promise and accusing the innocent of charges; and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A promise is a debt." So consider the excellence of truthfulness in this.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he used to enjoin on his people﴾ means by "them" his people and his community, as al-Hasan said. In the Mushaf of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads: "and he used to enjoin his people." And His saying "mardiyyan" (pleasing) originally was "mardwiyyun"; the waw came together with a sukun-bearing ya, so it was changed into a ya and assimilated, then the dad was kasra for harmony with the vowels. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: "and he was with his Lord mardwiyyan" [as "mardwiyyan" with alif of the accusative].

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And mention in the Book Idris. Indeed, he was truthful, a prophet.﴾ ﴿And We raised him to a high station.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones upon whom Allah bestowed favour from among the prophets, of the offspring of Adam, and of those whom We carried with Noah, and of the descendants of Abraham and Israel, and of those whom We guided and chose. When the verses of the Most Merciful were recited to them, they fell down in prostration and weeping.﴾

Idris (peace be upon him) is from the forefathers of Noah, and he is, as has been related, the first prophet sent to the people of the earth after Adam (may Allah's blessings be upon him). He was the first to write with the pen, and he was a tailor. Allah the Exalted described him with truthfulness (ṣidq), and the apparent meaning is that this is to be understood in general terms, covering both his sayings and his deeds. Ibn Masʿud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: he is Ilyas, who was sent to his people to tell them to say "There is no god but Allah" and to do whatever they wished, but they refused and were destroyed.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The more well-known view is that he was not sent to destroy a nation, and that he was a prophet only.

People have differed regarding His saying: ﴿And We raised him to a high station.﴾ A group of scholars said: this is the elevation of prophethood, honour, and rank, and he is in heaven just as the other prophets are. Another group said: rather, it is an elevation to the heavens. Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: this occurred by the command of Allah, just as Jesus (peace be upon him) was raised, and there Idris (peace be upon him) died. Mujahid said likewise, except that he said: "and he did not die." Wahb ibn Munabbih said likewise. Kaʿb al-Ahbar said to Ibn ʿAbbas: he had a friend among the angels who carried him on his wing and ascended with him until he reached the fourth heaven, where he met the Angel of Death. He said to him: "I have been told: descend to the fourth heaven and seize the soul of Idris, and I wonder how this can be." The ascending angel said to him: "This is Idris with me," and he took his soul. It is also related that all of this took place in the sixth heaven, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), and this is his rank in the narration of the Night Journey in some reports; whereas the hadith of Anas ibn Malik and Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with them both) concerning the Night Journey indicates that he was in the fourth heaven.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those are the ones upon whom Allah bestowed favour from among the prophets, of the offspring of Adam﴾ and the rest of the verse: the reference of "those" (ulāʾika) is to those previously mentioned. His saying "of the offspring of Adam" means Idris and Noah (peace be upon them both). "And of those whom We carried with Noah" means Abraham (peace be upon him). "And of the descendants of Abraham" means Ishmael, Isaac, and Jacob (peace be upon them all). "And Israel" means Moses, Aaron, Zechariah, John, and Jesus son of Mary (peace be upon them all). His saying "and of those whom We guided and chose" means: We selected and preferred. It seems to derive from "jabaytu al-māl" (I gathered the wealth), and from it comes "jibāyat al-māl" (collecting of taxes), as if the collector chooses it. Al-Jumhur recited "idhā tutlā" with the ta' from above, while Nafiʿ, Shaybah, and Abu Jaʿfar recited "idhā yutlā" with the ya'. "Al-āyāt" here means the revealed Books. "Sujjadan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl), because the beginning of prostration is itself prostration. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) and the majority recited "wa-bukiyyan." One group said: it is the plural of bākin (weeping), just as ʿātin and jāthin are pluralised as ʿutiyy and juthiyy. Another group said: it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) with the meaning of weeping, the implied sense being: "and they wept weeping." Al-Tabari and Makki argued for this view on the basis that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) is related to have recited Surah Maryam, prostrated, and then said: "This is the prostration, but where is the bukiyy?" meaning the weeping.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Their argument from this is flawed, because it is possible that ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) meant: "Where are the weepers?" so there is no proof in it for this view. And this report attributed to ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) was mentioned by Abu Hatim from the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Masʿud (may Allah be pleased with him), Yahya, and al-Aʿmash recited "wa-bikiyyan" with a kasra on the bāʾ, and on this reading it is a verbal noun that admits of no other meaning.

And they will have their provision therein morning and evening.﴾ ﴿That is the Paradise which We cause to inherit from Our servants those who were mindful of Allah.﴾

"Khalaf" (with a fatha on the lam) means a generation that comes after another that has passed away, or a son after his father, and it may be used for other matters generally. "Khalf" (with a sukun on the lam) is used when the one who comes after is blameworthy. This is the well-known usage of the Arabs. It has been reported from some of them that "khalaf" and "khalf" have the same meaning, and the evidence for this is the saying of the poet:

"For us is the first step towards You, and those who come after us follow our first in obedience to Allah."

The majority of readers recited ﴿أضاعوا الصلاة﴾ ("neglected the prayer") in the singular. Al-Hasan recited "أضاعوا الصلوات" ("neglected the prayers") in the plural, and it is the same in the codex of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him). By "khalf" is meant those among the Children of Israel who disbelieved or disobeyed after them. Mujahid said: the intended people are the Christians, who succeeded the Jews. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Mujahid, and 'Ata' said: they are a people of the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) at the end of time.

That is, there will be in this Ummah those who have this description, not that they are the intended ones in this verse. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "There will be a succession after sixty years."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

And this is a custom that will continue until the Day of Resurrection.

People differed about "neglecting the prayer" among them. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi and others said: it was neglect of disbelief and denial of it. Al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymira and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: it was neglecting its times and not being careful to observe its appointed hours. al-Tabari reported this from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz (may Allah be pleased with him) in a lengthy hadith. "Al-shahawat" (the desires) is general, and whatever is mentioned of that is an example.

"Al-ghayy" means loss and falling into destruction. From it is the saying of the poet:

"Whoever meets with good, people will praise his affair, and whoever goes astray will not lack a blamer for his error."

Ibn Zayd (may Allah have mercy on him) interpreted this verse in this sense. "Al-ghayy" may also mean misguidance, in which case there is an omitted word here, its implied meaning being: "they will meet the recompense of error." Al-Zajjaj interpreted it in this way. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "al-Ghayy" is a valley in Hell, and the threat in this verse refers to it. It was also said: "Al-ghayy and al-athām are two rivers in Hell," narrated by Abu Umama al-Bahili (may Allah be pleased with him) from the Prophet (ﷺ).

His saying ﴿except for those who repent﴾ is an exception which may be connected or disconnected. His saying ﴿and believe﴾ implies that the neglect mentioned first was neglect of disbelief, and this is the case when the exception is connected. al-Tabari interpreted it accordingly. The majority read "yudkhalūn" (they will be made to enter) with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the kha', while al-Hasan read every instance in the Qur'an as "yadkhulūn" (they will enter) with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the kha'.

As for His saying, Most High: ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾, the majority of readers recited "jannāti 'adnin" with the accusative on "jannāt," in apposition to His saying ﴿they will enter Paradise﴾. Al-Hasan, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, and Abu Haywa read it with the nominative, on the assumption of the implied "that is." 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) read "jannata" in the singular and accusative, and it is the same in the codex of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and al-A'mash also read it so. "Al-'adn" means permanent residence. His saying ﴿in the unseen﴾ means that He informed them of these things that were hidden from them. In this there is praise of them for the speed of their faith and their steadfastness, since they had not witnessed them. "Al-ma'tiyy" is a passive participle in its usual sense, and "al-ātī" (the thing that comes) is the fulfilment and the act contained in the promise, and its coming is intended only as the promise that preceded it. A group of the exegetes said: it is passive in form, but in meaning it is active: "āti" (coming).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is far-fetched, and the first view is more correct.

"Al-laghw" is idle speech, and it has various kinds, none of which are in Paradise. His saying ﴿except "Peace"﴾ is a disconnected exception, meaning: rather, they will hear "Peace." It is the greeting of the angels to them at all times. His saying ﴿morning and evening﴾ means, in terms of measurement, that their food comes to them twice within the span of a day and night. It is reported that the doors of Paradise are closed for them for the length of the night of this world, so they know morning by their opening and evening by their closing. Mujahid (may Allah have mercy on him) said: there is no morning or evening there, but they are given what they desire in this world.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Qatada mentioned something similar: that it is address in terms the Arabs know and find strange in the ease of living, and he took this as an expression that their provision comes in its most perfect form. al-Hasan said: they were addressed in terms of what the Arabs knew of the best living, since most Arabs would only find food once a day, and that was its limit, and the living of most of them came from the trees of the wilderness, from animals and the like. Do you not see the saying of the poet:

"Or a meal of the fruit of the thorny tree, which, unless he bends it with a bow, cannot be reached."

"Al-wajba" means one meal in a day.

The majority read "nūrithu" (We cause to inherit) with a sukun on the waw, while al-Hasan, al-A'raj, and Qatada read "nuwarrithu" with a fatha on the waw and a shadda on the ra'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 19, verses 64–65:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that. And your Lord is not forgetful.﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, so worship Him and be steadfast in His worship. Do you know of any similar to Him?﴾

The majority read "wa-ma natanazzalu" with the nun, as though Jibril (peace be upon him) was speaking of himself and the angels. Al-A'raj read "wa-ma yatanazzalu" with the ya', as a statement from God, Exalted, that Jibril does not descend. Some of the exegetes gave this interpretation, but the verse "To Him belongs what is before us" refutes it, because it does not fit with it. The reading more fitting is that it is a statement from Jibril (peace be upon him) that the Qur'an does not descend except by the command of God, blessed and exalted, at the times He decides. The reading of al-A'raj with a ḍammah on the ya' is also narrated. Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) read "illa bi-qawli rabbika" (except by the word of your Lord).

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) and others said: the occasion of this verse was that the Prophet (ﷺ) was delayed by Jibril once, and when he came, he said to him: "O Jibril, I have longed for you; will you not visit us more often than you visit us?" Then this verse was revealed.

Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: its occasion was that Jibril (peace be upon him) delayed from the Prophet (ﷺ) at his words in the earlier questions in Surah al-Kahf, "Tomorrow I will tell you," until the polytheists rejoiced at that, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was grieved. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) came, and this verse was revealed concerning that meaning, so it is like the one in al-Duha.

This "wa" in His saying "wa-ma natanazzalu" is a conjunction linking one speech to another, and connecting the two statements, even if their meanings are not the same. Al-Naqqash related from a people that His saying, exalted be He, "wa-ma natanazzalu" is connected to His saying: "I am only a messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy" [Maryam: 19].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a weak view.

His saying, exalted be He: "To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that" is an expression that requires three levels, and the exegetes differed concerning them. Abu al-'Aliya said: "what is before us" is the whole of the worldly life until the first blast; "what is behind us" is the Hereafter from the time of resurrection; and "what is between that" is what lies between the two blasts. Ibn Jurayj said: "what is before us" is the time that has passed before the creation of whoever is in the knowledge; "what is behind us" is what comes after their death until the continuation of the Hereafter; and "what is between that" is the duration of life.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The purpose of the verse is only to indicate God's dominion over His angels, and that their little and much activity is only by His command, and their movement from place to place is only for His service, since the places belong to Him and they belong to Him. If the verse is taken to mean that "what is before us and what is behind us" refers to the places in which they act, and that "what is between that" refers to themselves and their stations, its sense would be sound, as if He said: "We are bound by power; we do not move or descend except by the command of your Lord."

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, as narrated from them, and I do not think it is sound: "what is before us" is the Hereafter, and "what is behind us" is this world. The Qadi Abu Muhammad said:

This meaning is corrupt unless understood by way of likening it to place, as if what is before the hand is what has preceded in time, like the Torah and the Gospel relative to the Qur'an. Abu al-'Aliya's statement applies only to the children of Adam, whereas this statement concerns the angels, so reflect on it.

His saying, exalted be He: "And your Lord is not forgetful," meaning: He is not one who is subject to forgetfulness regarding sending Us to you at the time when it is beneficial for you; rather, that delay is according to a measure set by Him. That is, O Muhammad, do not seek a visit more than what God wills. This is what the strength of the speech requires on the first interpretation. Or: O Muhammad, do not be concerned about My delay, and do not turn to the rejoicing of the polytheists at that, on the second interpretation. "Nasiyyan" is on the pattern fa'il from forgetfulness and heedlessness regarding matters. A group said: "nasiyyan" means "one who abandons."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this there is weakness, because forgetfulness is negated absolutely, and this suits forgetfulness which is the explicit meaning, whereas abandonment is not absolutely negated. Do you not see His saying, blessed and exalted be He: "and He left them in darkness" [al-Baqarah: 17], and His saying: "And We left some of them that day surging against one another" [al-Kahf: 99]? So if He had said "nasiyaka" or something similar with a restriction, it would not be correct to take it to mean abandonment, and there is no need for us to say that the restriction is in the intention, because the other meaning is more apparent. Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) read: "wa-ma bayna dhalika wa-ma nasiyaka rabbuka." Abu al-Darda' narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "What Allah has made lawful in His Book is lawful, what He has made unlawful is unlawful, and what He has been silent about is pardoned, so accept it," then he recited this verse.

His saying, exalted be He: "Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them," the verse. "Rabb" is a substitute for His saying "wa-ma kana rabbuka." His saying: "so worship Him and be steadfast in His worship" is a command to bear the obligations of the Law and an indication of their difficulty, such as jihad, hajj, and charity; it is a law that requires steadfastness, which God help us to attain. The majority read "hal ta'lamu" with the lam made clear. 'Ali ibn Nasr narrated from Abu 'Amr that the lam was assimilated into the ta', and this is the reading of 'Isa, al-A'mash, al-Hasan, and Ibn Muhaysin. Abu 'Ali said: Sibawayh permits the assimilation of the lam into the ta', the ta', the dhal, the tha', the sad, the za', and the sin, and Abu 'Amr read "wa-hal thuwwiba" with its assimilation into the tha'; assimilation into the ta' is more appropriate, because it is closer to it in the mouth. Among its assimilation into the ta' is what is narrated from the words of Muzahim al-'Uqayli:

"Leave this aside, but will you help one infatuated, by the light of a flash of lightning that is far in the night, a watcher?"

His saying: "samiyyan." A group said, and this is the apparent meaning of the wording, that it means: "one who shares the name."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is fitting here that by "name" is meant what was mentioned earlier, His saying: "Lord of the heavens and the earth," meaning: do you know of anyone who is named by this and described by this attribute? For the nations do not name any idol or anything other than God, Exalted, with this name. As for divinity and power, the "samiyy" in them may be considered, but by homonymy, not by a single meaning. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "samiyyan" means "an equal, or a likeness, or the like."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a good view, and it seems that "samiyy" means one who rivals and matches, so it derives from "sumuww" (elevation). This view suits this verse but does not suit what was mentioned earlier concerning the mention of Yahya (peace be upon him).

**His saying, Exalted is He:**

﴿And man says, "When I have died, shall I really be brought forth alive?"﴾ ﴿Does not man remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?﴾ ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them, and the devils too, then We will surely bring them around Hell on their knees.﴾ ﴿Then We will surely draw out from every group whichever of them was most insolent toward the Most Merciful.﴾

"Al-insan" (mankind) is a generic noun, and what is meant by it is the disbelievers. It is reported that the reason for this verse is that men from Quraysh used to say this and similar things. It is also reported that the one who said it was Ubayy ibn Khalaf, who came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a crumbled bone, blew on it, and said, "Will this be raised?" He denied and mocked. It was also said that the one who said it was al-'As ibn Wa'il.

Al-A'raj and Abu 'Amr read "a-idha" (with the interrogative hamza clearly pronounced). A group read "idha" without the interrogative alif. This has already been discussed fully. A group read "mittu" with a kasra on the mim, and another group read it with a damma. The lam in His saying "la-sawfa" (surely) is brought in as a hikaya (a quotation, i.e. reporting of speech) of a previous statement with this meaning, as if someone had said to the disbeliever, "If you die, O so-and-so, you will surely be brought forth alive." So the disbeliever affirmed it in a manner of disbelief, and the statement is repeated as a hikaya of the first saying. Most people read "ukhraju" with a damma on the hamza. Al-Hasan (in one of the reported readings) and Abu Haywa read "akhruju" with a fatha on the hamza and a damma on the ra'.

His saying, "Does not man remember..." (to the end of the verse) is an argument. God, blessed and exalted, addressed His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), refuting the saying of the disbeliever. Nafi', 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "a-wa-la yadhkuru" (does he not remember), while Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "a-wa-la yadhdhakkaru" with the dhal and the kaf doubled. Ubayy ibn Ka'b (may Allah be pleased with him) read "a-wa-la yatadhakkaru." The first creation and bringing into existence from non-existence into being is the clearest proof of the possibility of resurrection from the graves. Then He established this and made it obligatory by revelation (al-sam'). In His saying, "and he was nothing," there is evidence that what does not exist is not called "a thing." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: He meant "a thing that exists."

**The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:**

This is a Mu'tazili tendency, so consider it carefully.

His saying, "So by your Lord, We will surely gather them..." (to the end of the verse) is a threat whose continuation is in its most severe forms. The pronoun in His saying "surely gather them" refers to the disbelievers who made the statements mentioned earlier. Then He informed that He will join with them the devils who led them astray. His saying "jithiyyan" (on their knees) is the plural of "jathin," like "qa'id" and "qu'ud," and "jalis" and "julus." Its original form is "juthuwwan." There is no unaccompanied final waw preceded by a damma in the speech of the Arabs, so it had to be altered. The intervening quiescent letter was not taken into account here because of its lightness and the scarcity of its surroundings, so it was changed into a ya', making it "juthuwiyyan." The waw and the ya' came together, and one of them was preceded by sukun, so it was changed into a ya'. Then the ya' was assimilated into the ya', and then the tha' was given a kasra to harmonize with the kasra and the ya'. The majority read "juthiyyan" and "saliyyan" with a damma on the jim and the sad. Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read "jithiyyan" and "saliyyan" with a kasra on the jim and the sad.

God, exalted, informed that He will bring these deniers of resurrection together with the devils, and they will kneel around Hell. This is the posture of a fearful, humiliated person on his knees, like a captive and the like. Qatada said: "Jithiyyan" means "on their knees." Ibn Zayd said: "Al-jithiyy" is the worst kind of sitting.

"Al-shi'a" is the group bound together by one doctrine, cooperating in it, as if some of them spread (yushi'u) others, meaning they alert them to it. From this comes "tashyi' al-nar" (kindling the fire) with firewood, which is feeding it with it little by little. From this it is said of a brave man: "mushi'u al-qalb" (one whose heart is kindled, i.e., steadfast). God informed that from every shi'a He will draw out the most stubborn and the most deserving of punishment, so that group will be the vanguard of their way to the Fire. Abu al-Ahwas said: The meaning is: We begin with the greatest in crime. Then God, exalted, informed in the verse afterwards that He is most knowing of who deserves that and most seeing, because their condition was not hidden from Him from its beginning to its end.

Some of the Kufans, Mu'adh ibn Muslim and Harun al-Qari read "ayyahum" with a fatha. The majority read "ayyuhum" with a damma. However, Talha and al-A'mash made the mim of "ayyuhum" quiescent. People differed about the reason for the raf' (nominative case) of "ayyu." Al-Khalil said: its raf' is by way of hikaya, with the implied meaning: "the one who is said of him, because of his arrogance, 'Which of them is most ...'" He compared this to the saying of the poet:

*"Indeed I spend the night with the young woman in a place, so I spend the night neither blamed nor deprived."*

That is, "so I spend the night while it is said of me: 'neither blamed nor deprived.'" Al-Zajjaj preferred al-Khalil's view. Al-Nahhas reported from him that he made an error in judgment regarding Sibawayh on this issue. Sibawayh said: "This would necessarily permit: 'I struck the thief, the wicked one,' meaning the one who is called that."

**The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:**

It is not necessary, because these are single nouns, while the verse is a sentence, and the governing of a verb over a single noun is stronger than over a sentence. Sibawayh's view is that "ayyuhum" is built on a damma, since it is a sister of "alladhi" and "ma." It differs from them in permitting an idafa (genitive construction), so it was declined for that reason. When the word that refers back to it was omitted from its relative clause, it became weak and reverted to being indeclinable. The implied meaning was: "ayyuhum huwa ashaddu" (which of them is the most ...). Abu 'Ali said: That which the sentence requires was omitted, so indeclinability became necessary. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 19, verses 70–72:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Then We are most knowing of those most deserving of burning therein.﴾ ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it. That is ever a decree of your Lord, a thing decreed.﴾ ﴿Then We will save those who feared Allah, and leave the wrongdoers therein kneeling.﴾

That is: We, in that drawing forth, do not place anything other than in its proper place, because We have encompassed everyone in knowledge. So We know who is most deserving of the burning of the Fire. The word "ṣilī" (burning) is a verbal noun of ṣalā, yaṣlā, meaning when one is in direct contact with it. Ibn Jurayj said: the meaning is "most deserving of remaining eternally (therein)."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾ is a certainty, and the "wāw" (and) requires it. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained it with his saying: "Whoever has three children who die before him, the Fire will not touch him except for the passing of an oath (taḥillat al-qasam)." 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), 'Ikrima, and a group read: "wa-in minhum" (with the pronoun hum), meaning the disbelievers.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

There is no dispute in this reading.

A group among the majority of readers read "minkum" (you), and the meaning is: say to them, O Muhammad, so the one addressed by "minkum" is the disbelievers.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The interpretation of these also is easy to grasp.

Most scholars said: the one addressed is the whole world, and all must pass over it. They differed over the manner in which the believers pass over it. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, Khalid ibn Ma'dan, Ibn Jurayj, and others said: it is a passing into it, but it will not harm the believers. Then Allah will bring them out of it after they know the reality of what they were saved from. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said on this matter to Nafi' ibn al-Azraq the Kharijite: "As for you and me, we must both pass over it. As for me, Allah will save me from it, and as for you, I do not think He will save you." They also said: there are four uses of "wurūd" in the Qur'an meaning entering. This is one of them. The second is His saying: ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them to the Fire﴾ [Hud: 98]. The third is His saying: ﴿And We will drive the criminals to Hell as a thirsty herd﴾ [Maryam: 86]. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 19, verse 73–75:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who disbelieve say to those who believe: "Which of the two groups is better in position and finer in assembly?"﴾ ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed before them, who were better in equipment and in appearance!﴾ ﴿Say: "Whoever is in error, the Most Merciful will extend for him an extension"﴾

Al-A'raj, Ibn Muhaysin, and Abu Haywa read "yutla" (is recited) with a yā' from below (yā' taḥtiyya, i.e., the verb is in the passive with a masculine-marked form of the verb, rather than the tā' form).

The occasion of this verse was that when a man among the disbelievers of Quraysh would speak with a believer about matters of the religion, and the believer would recite the Qur'an to him and overwhelm him with the verses of the Prophet (ﷺ), the disbeliever would say: "Allah only bestows goodness upon the most beloved of creation to Him, and He only grants blessings to the people of truth. Yet He has bestowed blessings upon us rather than you. We are rich and you are poor, our gathering is finer and our appearance more handsome." This meaning, and what is similar to it, is what is intended by the interrogative in His words: ﴿Which of the two groups?﴾

Nafi' and Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) read "maqāman" (مَقامًا) with a fatḥa on the mīm, and "lā maqāma lakum" (لا مَقامَ لَكُمْ) also with a fatḥa. It is either the verbal noun from qāma, or the place-noun from it in the sense of the place of standing. This would call for the word to be maqām, but the meaning in this verse makes clear that it refers only to the place (adverbial sense). Ubayy (may Allah be pleased with him) read: "fī muqāmin amīn" (فِي مُقامٍ أمِينٍ) with a ḍamma on the mīm. Ibn Kathir read "muqāman" (مُقامًا) with a ḍamma on the mīm, which is a place-noun from aqāma, and likewise the verbal noun from it, like "majrāhā wa mursāhā" (مَجْراها ومُرْساها). He read "fī maqāmin amīn" and "lā maqāma lakum" with a fatḥa. Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, Hamza, and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read all of them with a fatḥa. Ḥafṣ, from 'Asim, transmitted "lā muqāma lakum" with a ḍamma.

"Al-nadiyy" and "al-nādī" mean the assembly in which there is a group of people, and from it is the saying of Ḥātim al-Ṭā'ī:

؎ "And I was called among the foremost of the assembly, and they did not look at me with sidelong eyes."

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And how many have We destroyed before them﴾ are an address from Allah, Blessed and Exalted, to His Prophet Muḥammad (ﷺ). It is a statement that contains the breaking of their argument and the belittling of their affair, because the meaning is: this which they boast of has no worth with Allah and does not save them. So how many nations has Allah destroyed when they disbelieved, while they were stronger than these and had more wealth and a more handsome appearance. "Al-qarn" (generation): the community that is gathered in a single era. People differed over the length of time after which a community gathered is called a qarn: it was said one hundred years, it was said eighty years, and it was said seventy. This matter has been discussed before, more than once. "Al-athāth" (equipment): property, whether coin, goods, or animals, and it is a general noun. There is a difference as to whether it is a plural or a singular. Al-Farrā' said it is a collective noun with no singular from its own form, like "al-matā'" (goods). Khalaf al-Aḥmar said it is a plural whose singular is "athātha," like "ḥamāma" and "ḥamām" (pigeon and pigeons). From it is the saying of the poet:

؎ "Did the howdahs stir your longing on the day they departed, with the fine apparel and the equipment?"

Abu al-'Abbas recited:

؎ "Surely 'Uraynah knew, wherever they were, that we are the most numerous of them in equipment."

Nafi' — with a variant reading — and the people of Madina read "wariyyan" (وَرِيًّا) with a shaddah on the yā'. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), as transmitted from him, and Ṭalḥa read "wariyan" with a light yā'. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "wara'yan" (وَرَءْيًا) with a hamza followed by a yā', on the pattern of "ra'yan." It is also transmitted from Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir; Ashhab transmitted it from Nafi'. Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read "wari'an" (وَرِيئًا) with a sukūn on the yā' followed by a hamza, and this is by metathesis (qalb); its pattern is "fali'an," and it seems to be derived from "rā'a." The poet said:

؎ "Every friend who saw me says, because of you: 'This is the owl of today or tomorrow.'"

As for the two readings with hamza, they are from the sight of the eye: "al-ri'y" is the name of what is seen and what appears to the eye, like "al-ṭaḥn" and "al-saqy." Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-ri'y" is the appearance. Al-Ḥasan said: "wariyyan" has the same meaning. As for the one with the shaddah on the yā', it was said that it has the same meaning as the hamzated form, except that the hamza was lightened so that the endings of the verses would be even. Mundhir ibn Sa'id reported from some scholars that it is from "al-rayy" in irrigation, as if he meant that they were better than them in lands, more pleasant in terrain, and more abundant in blessings, since the totality of blessings is only from water and rain. As for the light-yā' reading, its basis is weak, and it has been said to be a solecism (laḥn). Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Yazid al-Barbari, and Ibn 'Abbas also read "wazyan" (وَزِيًّا) with a zāy, which means clothing and its appearance; one says "zuyyiyat," meaning "zayyanat" (she was adorned).

As for His words: ﴿Say: Whoever is in error﴾, it is a statement that may carry two meanings. The first is that it has the sense of supplication and entreaty, as if he says: whichever of us or of you is more misguided, may Allah extend for him until that leads to His punishment. The other meaning is that it has the sense of a report, as if he says: whoever among the nations is astray, Allah's custom with him is to extend for him and not hasten to him, until that leads to His punishment in the Hereafter.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So the lām in His words "falyamdud" (فَلْيَمْدُدْ), according to the first meaning, is the lām of request in the form of a command; and according to the second meaning, it is the lām of command that has entered upon the sense of a report, so that it is more emphatic and stronger. This exists in the speech of the Arabs and in their eloquence.

It is either the verbal noun from qāma, or the place-noun from it in the sense of the place of standing. This would call for the word to be maqām, but the meaning in this verse makes clear that it refers only to the place (adverbial sense). Ubayy (may Allah be pleased with him) read: "fī muqāmin amīn" (فِي مُقامٍ أمِينٍ) with a ḍamma on the mīm. Ibn Kathir read "muqāman" (مُقامًا) with a ḍamma on the mīm, which is a place-noun from aqāma, and likewise the verbal noun from it, like "majrāhā wa mursāhā" (مَجْراها ومُرْساها). He read "fī maqāmin amīn" and "lā maqāma lakum" with a fatḥa. Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, Hamza, and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read all of them with a fatḥa. Ḥafṣ, from 'Asim, transmitted "lā muqāma lakum" with a ḍamma.

"Al-nadiyy" and "al-nādī" mean the assembly in which there is a group of people, and from it is the saying of Ḥātim al-Ṭā'ī:

؎ "And I was called among the foremost of the assembly, and they did not look at me with sidelong eyes."

It is a statement that contains the breaking of their argument and the belittling of their affair, because the meaning is: this which they boast of has no worth with Allah and does not save them. People differed over the length of time after which a community gathered is called a qarn: it was said one hundred years, it was said eighty years, and it was said seventy. There is a difference as to whether it is a plural or a singular. Al-Farrā' said it is a collective noun with no singular from its own form, like "al-matā'" (goods). Khalaf al-Aḥmar said it is a plural whose singular is "athātha," like "ḥamāma" and "ḥamām" (pigeon and pigeons). From it is the saying of the poet:

؎ "Did the howdahs stir your longing on the day they departed, with the fine apparel and the equipment?"

Abu al-'Abbas recited:

؎ "Every friend who saw me says, because of you: 'This is the owl of today or tomorrow.'"
