Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 19, verses 76–80:

The words of the Exalted:

﴿Until, when they see that which they are promised, either the punishment or the Hour, then they will know who is worse in position and weaker in forces.﴾ [Maryam: 75] ﴿And Allah increases in guidance those who are guided, and the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in return.﴾ ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieves in Our signs and says, "I will surely be given wealth and children"?﴾ ﴿Has he looked into the unseen, or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?﴾ ﴿No! We will record what he says and extend for him of punishment an extension.﴾ ﴿And We will inherit from him what he says, and he will come to Us alone.﴾

"Ḥattā" (until) in this verse is a particle of beginning that enters upon a sentence, and it carries the meaning of a limit (ghāya). "Idhā" (when) is a conditional, and its response is in the words of the Exalted: ﴿then they will know﴾ [Maryam: 75]. "Al-ru'yah" is sight of the eye. "Al-'adhāb" and "al-sā'ah" are a substitution (badal) for "mā" upon which "ra'aw" falls. "Immā" is the one introduced for doubt at the beginning of the speech, and the second "immā" is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon it. By "al-ʿadhāb" he means the punishment of this world and the victory of the believers over them. "Al-jund" means victory and those who carry out the affair of war. "Sharr makānan" is in contrast to their saying "khayr maqāman," and "adʿaf jundan" is in contrast to their saying "aḥsan nadiyyan."

When he mentioned the misguidance of disbelief, and their confusion in being tested by the blessings of this world, and their blindness to the straight path, he followed that with mention of His blessing upon the believers: that He increases them in guidance in their adherence to righteous deeds, in knowledge of clear proofs, and in continual increase of knowledge. Al-Ṭabarī related from some of them: the meaning is through the abrogating and abrogated [verses] of the Qur'an.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an example.

"Al-bāqiyāt al-ṣāliḥāt" (the enduring good deeds) is an indication of that guidance which Allah increases them in, and these blessings upon them are better with Allah in reward and better in return.

The discussion regarding the increase of guidance is easy and its aspects are clear.

"Al-bāqiyāt al-ṣāliḥāt" is every righteous deed by which Allah raises the rank of its doer. Al-Ḥasan said: they are the obligatory duties (farā'iḍ). Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: they are the five prayers. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that they are the well-known words: Subḥān Allāh (Glory be to Allah), al-Ḥamdu lillāh (Praise be to Allah), Lā ilāha illā Allāh (There is no god but Allah), and Allāhu Akbar (Allah is greatest). The Prophet ﷺ said to Abū al-Dardā', may Allah be pleased with him: "Take them before they are barred between you and them, for they are the enduring good deeds, and they are among the treasures of Paradise." It is also related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said one day: "Take your shield (junnah)." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, from an enemy that has appeared?" He said: "From the Fire." They said: "What are they, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Subḥān Allāh, al-Ḥamdu lillāh, Lā ilāha illā Allāh, Allāhu Akbar, and they are the enduring good deeds." Abū al-Dardā', may Allah be pleased with him, whenever he mentioned this hadith, would say: "I will surely proclaim the tahlīl, and I will surely proclaim the takbīr of Allah, and I will surely glorify Him, until the ignorant one sees me and thinks I am mad."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieves in Our signs﴾. The fāʾ in His saying "afa-ra'ayta" is a conjunction after the interrogative alif, and it conjoins one sentence to another. The one ﴿who disbelieved﴾ is meant to be al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil al-Sahmī, as said by the majority of the exegetes. Its report: Khabbāb ibn al-Aratt was a smith in the Jāhiliyya, he performed a work for him, and a debt accumulated for him with him. He came to him seeking payment, and al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil said to him: "I will not pay you until you disbelieve in Muḥammad." Khabbāb said: "I will not disbelieve in Muḥammad, peace be upon him, until Allah causes you to die and then resurrects you." Al-ʿĀṣ said: "Will I be resurrected after death?" Khabbāb said: "Yes." He said: "Then when that happens, I will have wealth and children, and at that time I will pay you your debt." So the verse was revealed concerning that.

Al-Ḥasan said: the verse was revealed concerning al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Al-Walīd also had statements resembling this purpose.

Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr recited "wa-waladan" (وَوَلَدًا) with a fatḥa on the wāw and the lām, in the sense of the generic noun, and likewise throughout the Qur'an, except in Sūrat Nūḥ, where the two of them recited with a ḍamma on the wāw and a sukūn on the lām. Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn ʿĀmir recited with a fatḥa on the wāw throughout the Qur'an. Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī recited "wa-wuldan" (وَوُلْدًا) with a ḍamma on the wāw and a sukūn on the lām, likewise throughout the whole Qur'an. Ibn Masʿūd recited "wildan" (وِلْدًا) with a kasra on the wāw and a sukūn on the lām. As for the ḍamma on the wāw, there was disagreement: some said it is the plural of walad, like asad and usd, and they cited the words of the poet:

**Indeed I have seen companions who have multiplied wealth and offspring**

Others said it is singular, and they cited the words of the poet:

**Would that so-and-so had been in his mother's womb, and would that so-and-so had been the offspring of a donkey**

Abū ʿAlī, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In the recitation of Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī, whatever is singular is intended as singular, and whatever is plural is intended as plural. Al-Akhfash said: al-walad is the son, and al-wuld is the family and offspring. Others said: al-wuld is the lineage of the one who is from it; this is related by Abū ʿAlī in al-Ḥujjah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Has he looked into the unseen﴾ is a rebuke (tawqīf), and the alif is for interrogation, and it is elided in connected speech for being unnecessary. "Ittikhādh al-ʿahd" (taking a covenant) means: through faith and righteous deeds. "Kallā" is a restraint and a repudiation. Then Allah, the Exalted, informed that the saying of this disbeliever "sa-naktubu" (We will record), in the sense of preserving it against him and punishing him for it. ʿĀṣim and al-Aʿmash recited "sa-yuktabu" with a ḍamma on the yāʾ, and Abū ʿAmr, al-Ḥasan, and ʿĪsā recited "sa-naktubu" with the nūn. "Madd al-ʿadhāb" is its prolongation and magnification. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿what he says﴾ means: these things which he named, and said that he would be given them in the Hereafter. Allah inherits from him what he had of them in this world by destroying him and leaving them behind; so the inheritance is metaphorical, and it may be that his deprivation in the Hereafter is like the inheriting of what he hoped for. In the reading of Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him: "wa-narithuhu mā ʿindahu" (and We will inherit from him what is with him). Al-Naḥḥās said: "wa-narithuhu mā yaqūlu" means: We will preserve it against him in order to punish him. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets," that is, the preservers of what they said.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So it is as if this criminal bequeaths this statement. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and he will come to Us alone﴾ includes his humiliation.

In the reading of Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him: "wa-narithuhu mā ʿindahu" (and We will inherit from him what is with him). Al-Naḥḥās said: "wa-narithuhu mā yaqūlu" means: We will preserve it against him in order to punish him. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets," that is, the preservers of what they said.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So it is as if this criminal bequeaths this statement. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and he will come to Us alone﴾ includes his humiliation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 19, verses 81–87:

Allah's words, the Exalted, the Majestic:

﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah, that they may be for them a source of might.﴾ ﴿No! They will deny their worship of them and will become opposed to them.﴾ ﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with incitement?﴾ ﴿So do not be hasty against them; We are only counting for them a count.﴾ ﴿The Day We will gather the righteous to the Most Merciful as a delegation.﴾ ﴿And We will drive the criminals to Hell as a thirsty herd.﴾ ﴿They will not possess intercession, except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful.﴾

"Ittakhadha" is the form "if'tala" from "akhadha," but it implies a preparation by the one who takes for the one taken, which is not present in "akhadha." The pronoun in "ittakhadhu" refers to the worshippers of idols. "Al-ālihah" (the gods) are the idols and everything worshipped besides Allah, Blessed and Exalted. The meaning of "'izzan" (might) is general: support, benefit, and other aspects of good.

Allah's words "kallā" (no) are a rebuke and a rejection, and this meaning is necessarily carried by "kallā." If the statement being rejected is explicitly stated, the meaning becomes clear; if it is not explicitly stated, there must be an implied statement being rejected that the words contain. This is like the saying of Allah, the Majestic: ﴿Indeed, man transgresses﴾ [al-'Alaq: 6], for His words ﴿He taught man that which he did not know﴾ [al-'Alaq: 5], together with what precedes them, contain the implication that man claims for himself and thinks he has some power, and does not reflect deeply that Allah taught him what he did not know and bestowed this favour upon him.

The majority recited "kallā" as we have explained. Abu Nuhayk recited "kallan" with a fatha on the kaf and tanwin; Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinnī) transmitted this from him, and it is an adjective for "al-ālihah." Abu 'Amr al-Dani transmitted from him "kullan" with a damma on the kaf and tanwin, which is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb indicated by "sayakfurūna" (they will deny), its estimated form being: "they will reject," or "they will abandon," or "they will repudiate," or something similar.

The exegetes differed concerning the pronoun in "sayakfurūna" and in "bi-'ibādatihim" (their worship). One group said: the first refers to the disbelievers and the second to those worshipped, and the meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection there will come upon the disbelievers, from the terror and severity, what will push them to deny their disbelief and their worship of idols. This is like the saying of Allah, the Exalted, relating their words: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23]. Another group said: the first refers to those worshipped and the second to the disbelievers, and the meaning is that Allah, the Exalted, will give the idols a life by which they will deny the worship of the disbelievers and that they should bear some blame for it; as for those worshipped among the angels and others, their denial is clear. The words of Allah, the Exalted, "diddan" (opposed) mean: there will come from them (the idols) the opposite of what they had been hoped to be, and this will ultimately lead, for them, to a humiliation contrary to the might they had hoped for. This is a general description. Qatada said its meaning is "qurana'" (companions); Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said its meaning is "a'wānan" (helpers); al-Dahhak said "a'dā'" (enemies); Ibn Zayd said "balā'" (affliction). It has also been said other than this, while the wording of the Qur'an is more general than these and more comprehensive of the intended meaning. "Ḍidd" here is a verbal noun that describes a plural just as it describes a singular.

Al-Tabarī related from Abu Nuhayk that he recited "kullu" with a ḍamma (in the nominative) and took it as the subject (of a nominal sentence).

As for the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils﴾, the seeing is seeing of the heart. "Arsalnā" (We sent) means: We gave them power over them, or We did not stand between them and them, which is empowerment. This is like the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿We appoint for him a devil﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36]. Its construction with "'alā" (upon) indicates that it is empowerment. "Tauzzuhum" means: it disturbs them and moves them towards disbelief and error. Qatada said: it unsettles them with unsettling. Ibn Zayd said: it incites them with incitement, and from it comes "uzīr al-qidr," which is its boiling. From it is what is in the hadith: "I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and found him praying while weeping, and there was a sound in his chest like the sound of a boiling cauldron."

As for the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So do not be hasty against them﴾, meaning: do not seek to hasten their punishment and love its speeding up. And His words: ﴿We are only counting for them a count﴾ mean: the period of their blessings and the ugliness of their deeds, so that We may bring them to punishment, either in this world or, otherwise, in the Hereafter. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "We count their breaths."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What these expressions contain of the threat of the punishment of the Hereafter is what governs the words of Allah, "the Day" (yawma). It is possible that a hidden verb governs it, its estimated form being: "remember," or "beware," or something similar. "Al-ḥashr" (gathering) means assembling, and it has come to be used in the terminology of the sacred law to mean resurrection from the graves. Al-Hasan recited: "the Day when the righteous are gathered and the criminals are driven," and it was related from him: "wa-yasūqu al-mujrimīn." "Al-muttaqūn" (the righteous) are the believers whom Allah has forgiven.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of this "wifāda" (delegation) is that it occurs after the completion of the reckoning, and it is merely the rising towards Paradise; likewise, the "driving of the criminals" is for entering the Fire. As for "wafdan" (as a delegation), the exegetes said its meaning is: riding (on mounts), and this is the custom of delegations, because they are the nobles of the people and the best of them in appearance. So the people of Paradise are compared to them, not that they are in the sense of a delegation, since that implies departure; rather the intended meaning is to compare them to a delegation in bearing and honour. It was related from 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, that they will come riding on she-camels adorned with the adornment of Paradise, whose halters are of ruby and chrysolite and the like. It was related from 'Umar ibn Qays al-Mala'ī that they will ride on images made of their righteous deeds, which are in the utmost beauty. It was also related that each one of them will ride whatever he loves: some ride camels, some ride horses, and some ride ships, which will sail with them. It has been reported concerning sacrificial animals: "they are your mounts to Paradise." Much of this is far-fetched, but we have mentioned it for the sake of gathering the sayings. "Al-sawq" (driving) implies humiliation, because they are urged on from behind them. "Al-widr" means the thirsty, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayra and al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with them all.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

They are the people who are driven by thirst to come to water. It is possible that it is a verbal noun, meaning: "We will bring them as a bringing" (wirdan). Whoever sees in the Qur'an four instances of "awrād" (watering-places) makes it so, and this has been mentioned before.

The interpreters differed concerning the pronoun in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They do not possess﴾. One group said it refers to "the criminals," meaning: they do not possess that anyone should intercede for them, and there is no way for them to it. According to this interpretation, they are specifically polytheists, and His words, glorified be He: ﴿except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ are a disjunctive exception, meaning: "but whoever has taken a covenant, he will be interceded for." The "covenant" in this view is faith. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the covenant is "there is no god but Allah." In a hadith: "Allah, the Exalted, says on the Day of Resurrection: whoever has a covenant with Me, let him stand up." In a hadith: "Five prayers which Allah has prescribed for the servants; whoever comes with them complete, he has a covenant with Allah that He will admit him to Paradise." "Al-'ahd" also means faith, and by it was interpreted the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that "the criminals" comprises both disbelievers and sinners, and then He informed that they do not possess intercession, except the sinning believers, for they will be interceded for; in that case the exception is a connected one. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I will not cease to intercede until I say: O Lord, grant me intercession for whoever has said there is no god but Allah. Allah will say: O Muhammad, it is not for you, but it is for Me."

Another group said: the pronoun in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They do not possess﴾ refers to "the righteous," and His words: ﴿except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ mean: except one who has an outstanding righteous deed by which he is included among those who intercede. Hadiths have been repeatedly transmitted that people of knowledge, virtue and righteousness will be granted intercession and will intercede. It was related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Among my nation is a man through whose intercession Allah will admit more people into Paradise than the tribe of Tamīm." Qatada, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "We used to relate that a martyr will intercede for seventy."

Some of this group said: the meaning of the speech is: "except for one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful," meaning: the righteous do not possess intercession except for this select group. So "man" in the first interpretation refers to the intercessors, and in the second to those for whom intercession is made.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The verse may also mean by "man" Muhammad (ﷺ), and by "intercession" the special intercession belonging to him (ﷺ) which is general for the people, and the pronoun in "yamlikūna" refers to all the people of the standing place. Do you not see that all the other prophets will push away the intercession until it reaches him, and then he (ﷺ) rises to it? So the "covenant" in this view is the explicit statement concerning the matter of intercession in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ [al-Isra': 79].

Allah's words "kallā" (no) are a rebuke and a rejection, and this meaning is necessarily carried by "kallā." If the statement being rejected is explicitly stated, the meaning becomes clear; if it is not explicitly stated, there must be an implied statement being rejected that the words contain. This is like the saying of Allah, the Majestic: ﴿Indeed, man transgresses﴾ [al-'Alaq: 6], for His words ﴿He taught man that which he did not know﴾ [al-'Alaq: 5], together with what precedes them, contain the implication that man claims for himself and thinks he has some power, and does not reflect deeply that Allah taught him what he did not know and bestowed this favour upon him.

The majority recited "kallā" as we have explained. Abu Nuhayk recited "kallan" with a fatha on the kaf and tanwin; Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinnī) transmitted this from him, and it is an adjective for "al-ālihah." Abu 'Amr al-Dani transmitted from him "kullan" with a damma on the kaf and tanwin, which is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb indicated by "sayakfurūna" (they will deny), its estimated form being: "they will reject," or "they will abandon," or "they will repudiate," or something similar.

The exegetes differed concerning the pronoun in "sayakfurūna" and in "bi-'ibādatihim" (their worship). One group said: the first refers to the disbelievers and the second to those worshipped, and the meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection there will come upon the disbelievers, from the terror and severity, what will push them to deny their disbelief and their worship of idols. This is like the saying of Allah, the Exalted, relating their words: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23]. Another group said: the first refers to those worshipped and the second to the disbelievers, and the meaning is that Allah, the Exalted, will give the idols a life by which they will deny the worship of the disbelievers and that they should bear some blame for it; as for those worshipped among the angels and others, their denial is clear. The words of Allah, the Exalted, "diddan" (opposed) mean: there will come from them (the idols) the opposite of what they had been hoped to be, and this will ultimately lead, for them, to a humiliation contrary to the might they had hoped for. This is a general description. Qatada said its meaning is "qurana'" (companions); Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said its meaning is "a'wānan" (helpers); al-Dahhak said "a'dā'" (enemies); Ibn Zayd said "balā'" (affliction). It has also been said other than this, while the wording of the Qur'an is more general than these and more comprehensive of the intended meaning. "Ḍidd" here is a verbal noun that describes a plural just as it describes a singular.

Al-Tabarī related from Abu Nuhayk that he recited "kullu" with a ḍamma (in the nominative) and took it as the subject (of a nominal sentence).

As for the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils﴾, the seeing is seeing of the heart. "Arsalnā" (We sent) means: We gave them power over them, or We did not stand between them and them, which is empowerment. This is like the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿We appoint for him a devil﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36]. Its construction with "'alā" (upon) indicates that it is empowerment. "Tauzzuhum" means: it disturbs them and moves them towards disbelief and error. Qatada said: it unsettles them with unsettling. Ibn Zayd said: it incites them with incitement, and from it comes "uzīr al-qidr," which is its boiling. From it is what is in the hadith: "I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and found him praying while weeping, and there was a sound in his chest like the sound of a boiling cauldron."

As for the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So do not be hasty against them﴾, meaning: do not seek to hasten their punishment and love its speeding up. And His words: ﴿We are only counting for them a count﴾ mean: the period of their blessings and the ugliness of their deeds, so that We may bring them to punishment, either in this world or, otherwise, in the Hereafter. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "We count their breaths."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What these expressions contain of the threat of the punishment of the Hereafter is what governs the words of Allah, "the Day" (yawma). It is possible that a hidden verb governs it, its estimated form being: "remember," or "beware," or something similar. "Al-ḥashr" (gathering) means assembling, and it has come to be used in the terminology of the sacred law to mean resurrection from the graves. Al-Hasan recited: "the Day when the righteous are gathered and the criminals are driven," and it was related from him: "wa-yasūqu al-mujrimīn." "Al-muttaqūn" (the righteous) are the believers whom Allah has forgiven.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of this "wifāda" (delegation) is that it occurs after the completion of the reckoning, and it is merely the rising towards Paradise; likewise, the "driving of the criminals" is for entering the Fire. As for "wafdan" (as a delegation), the exegetes said its meaning is: riding (on mounts), and this is the custom of delegations, because they are the nobles of the people and the best of them in appearance. So the people of Paradise are compared to them, not that they are in the sense of a delegation, since that implies departure; rather the intended meaning is to compare them to a delegation in bearing and honour. It was related from 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, that they will come riding on she-camels adorned with the adornment of Paradise, whose halters are of ruby and chrysolite and the like. It was related from 'Umar ibn Qays al-Mala'ī that they will ride on images made of their righteous deeds, which are in the utmost beauty. It was also related that each one of them will ride whatever he loves: some ride camels, some ride horses, and some ride ships, which will sail with them. It has been reported concerning sacrificial animals: "they are your mounts to Paradise." Much of this is far-fetched, but we have mentioned it for the sake of gathering the sayings. "Al-sawq" (driving) implies humiliation, because they are urged on from behind them. "Al-widr" means the thirsty, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayra and al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with them all.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

They are the people who are driven by thirst to come to water. It is possible that it is a verbal noun, meaning: "We will bring them as a bringing" (wirdan). Whoever sees in the Qur'an four instances of "awrād" (watering-places) makes it so, and this has been mentioned before.

The interpreters differed concerning the pronoun in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They do not possess﴾. One group said it refers to "the criminals," meaning: they do not possess that anyone should intercede for them, and there is no way for them to it. According to this interpretation, they are specifically polytheists, and His words, glorified be He: ﴿except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ are a disjunctive exception, meaning: "but whoever has taken a covenant, he will be interceded for." The "covenant" in this view is faith. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the covenant is "there is no god but Allah." In a hadith: "Allah, the Exalted, says on the Day of Resurrection: whoever has a covenant with Me, let him stand up." In a hadith: "Five prayers which Allah has prescribed for the servants; whoever comes with them complete, he has a covenant with Allah that He will admit him to Paradise." "Al-'ahd" also means faith, and by it was interpreted the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that "the criminals" comprises both disbelievers and sinners, and then He informed that they do not possess intercession, except the sinning believers, for they will be interceded for; in that case the exception is a connected one. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I will not cease to intercede until I say: O Lord, grant me intercession for whoever has said there is no god but Allah. The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The verse may also mean by "man" Muhammad (ﷺ), and by "intercession" the special intercession belonging to him (ﷺ) which is general for the people, and the pronoun in "yamlikūna" refers to all the people of the standing place. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 19, verses 88–96:**

The Almighty said:

﴿They say, "The Most Merciful has taken to Himself a son."﴾ ﴿Indeed you have produced a monstrous thing.﴾ ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder because of it, the earth is split open, and the mountains collapse in ruin,﴾ ﴿because they attribute a son to the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿It is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take to Himself a son.﴾ ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but comes to the Most Merciful as a servant.﴾ ﴿He has indeed encompassed them and counted them with exact counting.﴾ ﴿And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, the Most Merciful will bestow love upon them.﴾

The pronoun in "qalu" (they say) refers to the disbelievers among the Arabs, in their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah, and to the Christians, and to everyone who disbelieves in this kind of disbelief. His saying "laqad ji'tum" (indeed you have produced), after the indirect reference to them, means: "Say to them, O Muhammad." "Al-idd" is a grievous and difficult matter, namely calamities and great abominations. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that this statement, the first time it was uttered in the world, caused the trees to bristle, Hell to blaze up, and the angels to become angry. (p-72) The majority recited "iddan" with a kasra on the hamza. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman recited "adddan" with a fatha on the hamza. It is also said "idd," "udd," and "ādd." Ibn Kathir recited here, and in "'Asaq," "takadu" with a ta', "yatafattarna" with a ya' and a ta', with a fatha on the ta' and a shadda on it; Hafs related it from 'Asim. Abu 'Amr and 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, recited "takadu" with a ta', "yanfatirna" with a ya' and a nun, with a kasra on the ta'. Nafi' and al-Kisa'i recited "yakadu" with a ya' and the removal of the feminine marker, "yatafattarna" with a ya' and a ta', with a shadda and a fatha on the ta' in both places. Hamza and Ibn 'Amir, in Maryam, recited like Abu 'Amr, and in "'Asaq" like Ibn Kathir. Abu al-Hasan and al-Akhfash said: "yakadu" here means "yuridu" (intends), and similarly the Most High's saying: ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15]. They cited, as evidence that "kada" means "arada" (intended), the words of the poet:

*"She intended, and I intended, and that is the best intention; if only there returned from the time of passion what has passed."*

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no proof in this verse, and this view is unsound.

The majority said: it is only a metaphor for the enormity of the matter, that is, this is its due if the inanimate things could comprehend its magnitude. This meaning is common among the Arabs. From it is the saying of Jarir:

*"When the news of al-Zubayr came, the walls of the city and the humbled mountains were humbled."*

And from it is the saying of another:

*"Did you not see a crack in the sky made manifest over the son of the Banu al-Harith ibn Hisham?"*

And another said:

*"The valley of Makkah became horrified, as if the earth had no Hisham in it."*

"Al-infitar" is splitting along an unintended line, and "al-hadd" is collapse and scattering swiftly. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the enemies of Allah almost caused the Hour to be established against us.

His saying the Most High: ﴿It is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take to Himself a son﴾ is a negation by way of exalting Him above that. This meaning and the categories of this expression have already been mentioned in this surah.

His saying: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth…﴾ is the verse. "In" is a negation in the sense of "ma." The majority recited "ati al-Rahman" with the genitive construction. Talha recited "atin al-Rahmana" with tanwin on "atin" and the accusative on the nun. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, recited "lama ati al-Rahman." Some people used this verse as evidence that a son cannot be a servant.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This inference is far-fetched, and "'abdan" is a circumstantial accusative.

Then He informed, exalted is He, of His encompassing and knowledge of His servants, mentioning "al-ihsa'" (enumeration), then repeated the meaning in other words. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, recited: "laqad katabahum wa 'addahum," and in the codex of Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him: "laqad ahsahum fa-ajmalahum 'adadan." His saying "'addan" is an emphasis on the verb and its confirmation. His saying "fardan" implies the meaning of having no help, no power, and no strength, with no protector from what Allah wills for him.

His saying the Most High: ﴿The Most Merciful will bestow love upon them.﴾ Most of the exegetes held that this is the acceptance that Allah places for whomever He loves among His servants, according to what is in the transmitted hadith. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is in the same position as the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever keeps a secret, Allah clothes him in its cloak." In the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no servant but that he has a reputation in the heavens; if it is good, it is placed on the earth as good, and if it is evil, it is placed likewise."

"'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the verse was revealed concerning him, because when he migrated from Makkah he felt lonely in Madinah, so he complained of that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the verse was revealed concerning that." That is: the souls of the believers will settle and they will love their state and station. Al-Naqqash mentioned that it was revealed concerning 'Ali ibn (p-75) Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. Ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: there is no believer but that he loves 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and the people of his household, may Allah be pleased with them.

The majority recited "wuddan" with a damma on the waw. Abu al-Harith al-Hanafi recited it with a fatha on the waw.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The verse may be connected in meaning to what precedes it, meaning: when Allah, blessed and exalted is He, informed of the coming of everyone in the heavens and the earth in the state of servitude and solitude, He gave the believers comfort by saying that He will bestow upon them on that Day "wuddan," which is what manifests of His honour upon them; for Allah's love for the servant is what He manifests upon him of His blessings and the signs of His forgiveness of him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 19, verses 97–98:

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿So We have only made it easy in your tongue, that you may give good tidings thereby to the righteous and warn thereby a people given to contention.﴾ ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed before them? Do you perceive any of them or hear from them a whisper?﴾

The pronoun in "yassarnā" (We made easy) refers to the Qur'an. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until it [the sun] was hidden behind the veil﴾ [Sad: 32]. The meaning necessitates what is intended even though it has not been mentioned before. The facilitation consisted in its being in the tongue of Muhammad ﷺ, in his language, which is understood and clarifying. The good tidings for the righteous (al-muttaqūn) are Paradise, everlasting bliss, and honour in this world. "Al-qawm al-luddu" (a people given to contention) are the Quraysh. Its meaning: arguing and disputing with falsehood; and al-aladd (one who is contentious) is the disputant who exceeds in that. Mujahid said: "luddan" means "fujjāran" (wicked, profligate).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view this is the wickedness of disputation, and none is contentious (yaliddu) except the one who is in falsehood. And in a hadith: «The most hateful of men to Allah is the alad, the disputatious adversary.»

Then, when Allah the Exalted described them as luddun (contentious), which is a description of evil by the judgment of the Sharia and of truth, it was necessary that He harden His address against them with the threat and with the example of the destruction of those who were stronger than them, more contentious, and greater in standing, those who would have been pleased in themselves by the description "ludd" (contentious). For the Arabs, in their ignorance, arrogance and disbelief, used to boast of contentiousness and regard it as perception and nobility. Among this is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed beneath the stones are resolve and firmness, and an adversary most contentious, closed-minded."

So He presented to them the example of the destruction of those before them, so that they would belittle themselves and it would become clear how small their station is. The commentators rendered "ludd" as "fajara" (wicked) and "zalama" (unjust), and the summary of its meaning is what we have mentioned.

"Al-qarn" is the community (ummah), and "al-rikz" is the faint sound without speech in letters and without a mouth; it is only the sound of movements and their rustling. From it is the saying of Labid:

"And she sensed the rikz of a companion and was startled by it, from behind the unseen, and the companion was her sickness."

So it is as if He said: Do you hear from their news anything, little or much, or a faint, weak trace? This is meant to refer to those whose affair has passed among the nations and whose report has faded. It may also be understood to mean: Does any of them remain, with speech or with any kind of trace? Thus included in this is anyone whose destruction is known among the nations.

Here ends the tafsir of Surat Maryam, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 19, verses 97–98:

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿So We have only made it easy in your tongue, that you may give good tidings thereby to the righteous and warn thereby a people given to contention.﴾ ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed before them? Do you perceive any of them or hear from them a whisper?﴾

The pronoun in "yassarnā" (We made easy) refers to the Qur'an. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until it [the sun] was hidden behind the veil﴾ [Sad: 32]. The meaning necessitates what is intended even though it has not been mentioned before. The facilitation consisted in its being in the tongue of Muhammad ﷺ, in his language, which is understood and clarifying. The good tidings for the righteous (al-muttaqūn) are Paradise, everlasting bliss, and honour in this world. "Al-qawm al-luddu" (a people given to contention) are the Quraysh. Its meaning: arguing and disputing with falsehood; and al-aladd (one who is contentious) is the disputant who exceeds in that. Mujahid said: "luddan" means "fujjāran" (wicked, profligate).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view this is the wickedness of disputation, and none is contentious (yaliddu) except the one who is in falsehood. And in a hadith: «The most hateful of men to Allah is the alad, the disputatious adversary.»

Then, when Allah the Exalted described them as luddun (contentious), which is a description of evil by the judgment of the Sharia and of truth, it was necessary that He harden His address against them with the threat and with the example of the destruction of those who were stronger than them, more contentious, and greater in standing, those who would have been pleased in themselves by the description "ludd" (contentious). For the Arabs, in their ignorance, arrogance and disbelief, used to boast of contentiousness and regard it as perception and nobility. Among this is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed beneath the stones are resolve and firmness, and an adversary most contentious, closed-minded."

So He presented to them the example of the destruction of those before them, so that they would belittle themselves and it would become clear how small their station is. The commentators rendered "ludd" as "fajara" (wicked) and "zalama" (unjust), and the summary of its meaning is what we have mentioned.

"Al-qarn" is the community (ummah), and "al-rikz" is the faint sound without speech in letters and without a mouth; it is only the sound of movements and their rustling. From it is the saying of Labid:

"And she sensed the rikz of a companion and was startled by it, from behind the unseen, and the companion was her sickness."

So it is as if He said: Do you hear from their news anything, little or much, or a faint, weak trace? This is meant to refer to those whose affair has passed among the nations and whose report has faded. It may also be understood to mean: Does any of them remain, with speech or with any kind of trace? Thus included in this is anyone whose destruction is known among the nations.

Here ends the tafsir of Surat Maryam, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
